1881223,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.3.2.8.2,1957-01-24,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,UNITED STATES DISPOSAL POLICY-PROTESTS BY CANADA,Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce arising out of the report of a speech he made last evening at the Seigniory club with regard to what was described as the rough disposal policy of the United States? It had to do with the fire sale, giveaway policy with respect to agricultural products and in particular wheat.

I should like to ask the minister this question. When was the last protest made to the United States against this type of disposal program, which violates GATT and the resolution of FAO, and what reply was received to that latest protest? Was the protest in writing? If so, would the minister table that protest and the reply?

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL
1881224,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.3.2.8.3,1957-01-24,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):,Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce,INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,UNITED STATES DISPOSAL POLICY-PROTESTS BY CANADA,Mr. Speaker, the two governments have appointed a continuing committee of senior civil servants of both governments to deal with these matters. The committee meets from time to time. I think the last meeting was some two or three weeks ago. Protests are filed through that committee, and sometimes remedial action is taken. Protests, I may say, are sometimes filed in both directions. In any event we find that committee has been useful as a means of conveying our protests, and has had some effect in discouraging certain policies to which we in Canada take strong objection. There is nothing to table. We do not file our protests in writing; we file them through the committee.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1881225,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.3.2.8.4,1957-01-24,84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089,ca.m.3212,Mr. Diefenbaker:,Leader of the Official Opposition,INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS,EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,UNITED STATES DISPOSAL POLICY-PROTESTS BY CANADA,Would the minister say what changes have been made in consequence oi the complaints that have been made to the United States government through this committee? Would the minister also say what is being done so that Canada may recover her position as the leading exporter of wheat, a position which has been seriously endangered as a result of United States action?

,Progressive Conservative,,John George Diefenbaker,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=84909dc1-9a60-44b3-a939-2393ab563089&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL

The making of an announcement outside of the house is much worse than making it in the house. I wanted to get particulars. Possibly I shall direct my question to the Prime Minister in order to get information on this matter. I ask him whether when he last met President Eisenhower and brought to the President's attention the serious situation brought about by the trade balance between Canada and the United States, which caused shock to the President when he found it out, he also let the President know how utterly unjust and unfair it is for the United States to carry on this disposal policy to the detriment of fair competition on the part of Canada?

Hahn (New Westminster):,,POULTRY,REQUEST FOR MODIFICATION OF INSPECTION REGULATIONS,,Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. Is the minister aware that the health of animals inspection regulation requiring a minimum of 10,000 birds per week is being exploited to advantage by three large poultry processing plants in British Columbia, who are labelling their product ""H of A approved"" and in so doing are even now capturing the poultry market in that province by implying that smaller plants do not meet federal health standards despite the fact that their standards of health inspection are equal to or surpass federal requirements? If so, will the minister immediately consider modifying such regulation's and allow all processing
plants meeting such health requirements to label their products ""H of A approved""?

,Social Credit,,Frederick George Hahn,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=c7ae0236-fd24-4936-904c-ad8d3b4f9214&Language=E&Section=ALL

Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):,Minister of Agriculture,POULTRY,REQUEST FOR MODIFICATION OF INSPECTION REGULATIONS,,Mr. Speaker, I was handed this question just as I came into the house. I can only say I was not aware of all the things happening that are mentioned in the question.

The facts are that in all these matters we have inspectors in plants that carry on export trade in the commodities concerned. We have no authority to have similar inspections made in other, smaller plants that buy and sell practically all their products within a province. There is no inspector put in plants by the health of animals branch, until they have been approved under provincial health requirements. Therefore any ""H of A approved"" marking that is put on the products is put on following provincial inspection.

In other words these must be plants that are approved by the provincial authority as putting up the products under conditions set by the provincial health regulations, and that part of it is taken care of before we enter into inspection at all. Our inspection and marking indicates that it has been checked by our people, and is to satisfy the regulations in connection with export. All the other matters having to do with the smaller plants concern the provincial authority.

,Liberal,,James Garfield Gardiner,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b88f8c1a-3837-4be1-8acb-61fedd1a9cc1&Language=E&Section=ALL

In view of the fact that the inspection in these plants is particularly for export purposes, and since the product is being used in the domestic market, would the minister therefore approve of the provincial body allowing the domestic use of the same ""H of A approved"" stamp in the small provincial plants?

,Social Credit,,Frederick George Hahn,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=c7ae0236-fd24-4936-904c-ad8d3b4f9214&Language=E&Section=ALL

They insist on inspection being made by the federal authority in connection with products they import; but the choice is made not by this government but rather by the individual operators of the packing plants, whether they process poultry or some other product; and if they do intend to export then they apply for inspection on the part of our authorities. If they do not intend to export they do not apply for federal inspection.

Marler (Minister of Transport):,Minister of Transport,TRANSPORT,FERRY "CABOT STRAIT",STATEMENT AS TO REFLOATING,Yesterday the hon. member for Queens inquired as to what progress was being made in efforts to refloat the S. S. Cabot Strait, and also asked for comment on the adequacy of the substitute service provided.

I am advised by the management of the Canadian National Railways that salvage operations are under way but that the vessel has not yet been refloated. With regard to substitute service, the management advises that the motor vessel Nonia is operating in place of the disabled ship, and daily service has not been interrupted. 1881354,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.1,1957-01-24,,,,subtopic,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,,,['Thank you, Mr. Speaker. There is no necessity to quote what the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said. The only reason I was using his words was that they expressed what I wanted to say so much better than I could myself. The point I was trying to make was that there is considerable difference between the objectives of this resolution and those of the other measure to which I referred and which also envisages grants and scholarships to students. In introducing the resolution having to do with the Canada Council the Prime Minister pointed out that scholarships would be made available to people who perhaps could not properly be considered as university students. He went on to illustrate that by mentioning groups of people such as artists, musicians and actors.

The resolution which we are now considering is different in two very important respects. In the first place, it is different in that it is specifically designed to help needy students to get a university education. The factor of need does not enter into the awarding of scholarships under the Canada Council. It is also different in that it makes provision for bursaries as well as scholarships which the other measure does not. One might have hoped that this resolution would have also made provision for the granting of interest free loans to students.
It is fitting that education should occupy the attention of this house to such a great extent at this time. Canada is a very rich country with a tremendous future and education is essential to the development of our material resources and the steady expansion of our economy. Education can also play a very important part in the development of those areas of our country which may not be so richly blessed with natural wealth.
We all think of the United States, our neighbour to the south, as having the highest standard of living in the world. Mr. Thomas Bouchel, a member of the United States chamber of commerce, when addressing audiences in the United States following his return from Europe some time ago has been quoted as saying that in his opinion Switzerland has the highest standard of living in the world and Denmark had the highest standard of life.
In recent months we have become increasingly conscious of the fact that university education is also essential to our national defence.
Indeed it may even be our first line of defence. The emphasis which Russia is placing on education and the feverish haste of Russian universities to turn out engineers and scientists indicate that they have made the same appraisal. It becomes increasingly clear that our human resources, our brain power, are the most precious of all our resources. Any nation which neglects their development does so at its own peril.
On the political level education is essential also to the preservation of our democracy and our democratic institutions and to the solving of the complex problems which face us today. Democracy has been described as government of the people, by the people, for the people. Democracy cannot work unless the people are in position to play their part effectively, and they cannot play their part effectively without sufficient educational training to develop independent thought and judgment.
The people must be able to understand the present in the terms of the past and to

anticipate the future in terms of both. Abraham Lincoln said that ""if we could just know where we are and whither we are tending, we could better know what to do and how to do it."" Above all education is essential for living a life. The only forms of life that have survived on this planet are those which have been successful in adapting themselves to their environment. In this age of electronics, automation and the atom bomb the ability to adapt oneself to one's environment becomes more vital still. A knowledge and appreciation of those values which satisfy the soul, which go to make up a full life and which are of permanent lasting value are indispensable if people and
Education
nations are to reverse their present course toward chaos and destruction.
On motion of Mr. Carter the debate was adjourned.']",,,,

1881355,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.1.1,1957-01-24,ed24e5ee-f2d9-4323-a652-85ff86e54e54,ca.m.5158,Mr. Speaker:,Speaker of the House of Commons,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,,,"I think I am in duty bound to say something about the manner in which questions are being asked. I am sure there is on the part of hon. members a sincere desire to observe the rules. Standing order 39 (1) reads as follows:

39. (1) Questions may be placed on the order paper seeking information from ministers of the crown relating to public affairs: and from other members, relating to any bill, motion, or other public matter connected with the business of the house, in which such members may be concerned; but in putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as may be necessary to explain the same; and in answering any such question the matter to which the same refers shall not be debated.
Citation 297 of Beauchesne's third edition is to the following effect:

297. A certain number of oral questions are permitted in practice by members, without notice, before the orders of the day are called; but these are merely allowed by courtesy in connection with the business of the house or with very urgent and important matters of public concern. They are always brief, no debate being permitted, and the replies are as concise as possible. The minister interrogated may reply at once or may direct that the usual notice be given. Such questions are governed by the same rules of order as questions of which notice has been given.

Therefore, if oral questions are to be governed by the same rules of order as questions of which notice has been given, they are subject to the following rule found in standing order 39 (1), the last part of which I will read again:

. . . but in putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to be offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as may be necessary to explain the same; and in answering any such question the matter to which the same refers shall not be debated.
There are other citations in Beauchesne which further explain what the practice should be. I should like to cite citation 311, which reads as follows:

311. Although there may be no debate on an answer, further questions, within due limits, may be addressed to the minister as may be necessary for the elucidation of the answers that have been given. The extent to which supplementary questions may be asked is in the discretion of the Speaker.
After a minister has answered a question asked by a member when the orders of the day are called, no discussion of any kind should take place.

Then it goes on to cite a statement by Mr. Speaker Lowther in 1915 which I will not read to this house, but it is there for hon. members to consult. Citation 295 gives the details of the various rulings that have been made by my predecessors on questions asked from time to time over the years. I would also mention citations 296, 298, 299, 300, 301 and 302.

Last year I made a statement with regard to questions after having made a study of the matter, and it was my hope that the statement I made then, which was lengthy, would be the last one that I should be obliged to make. See Journals, Friday, 16th March, 1956, pages 299-305. I think it is obvious to any hon. gentleman that we may be departing from the requirements of the rules as they actually exit. I believe hon. members will agree, and this is my own view, that at question time I have been so lenient that some hon. members may have felt justified in addressing to me serious reproaches for my lack of vigilance at that stage of the proceedings. I am not going to divulge private conversations, but certain members on both sides of the house have often told me that at question time they were ""getting away with murder"".

They know what the rules are. We all know what they are. We also know how much more entertaining it may be to have more latitude than the rules allow. But the rules as they stand are the rules I must apply, no matter how much perhaps I personally should like to see another system established. The only way the rules can be changed is by the house itself through a committee on procedure, which would recommend certain changes and have them debated. If hon. members do not like this type of procedure-I refer to the one that is provided for-they may take the steps that are necessary to have it changed. See Beauchesne's third edition, citations 9 and 10.
What I have said today does not apply to any questions that have been asked today in particular. My remarks are not addressed

to any hon. member in particular. I am not admonishing the house. I am not reprimanding anyone. I am just speaking in general as to the manner in which we have conducted ourselves, and I include members of the opposition and members of the government as well. The rules are to the effect that the replies must be concise and should not include any more facts than are necessary to give the reply. The rule applies to the question and it applies to the reply. I include myself in the remarks I have been making, because I perhaps should have been more vigilant in the interpretation and observance of the rules.

Having in mind the ambition that we all have to respect our rules, let us resolve that if we do not like them we shall change them in the manner which is provided under our rules. Let us hope we can carry on from here. I hope we may have interesting question periods just the same, but that we shall keep within the rules.

SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,"That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide national scholarships and bursaries for students at the university level who are in financial need in so far as the subject matter of this resolution is within the competence of parliament.

He said: I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to again sponsor this resolution, which has as its objective the assistance to university students in financial need by means of bursaries and scholarships. I should like to say at this time how very much I appreciate the widespread support I received in the house last year when this resolution came up for the first time. I suppose that is as it should be, because this particular crusade is essentially non-partisan. I should like also to compliment the national federation of Canadian university students for the untiring work they have done in this regard, and I would think the work in which they have persevered throughout the years will soon bear fruit.

There seems to be a considerable amount of confusion in the minds of many people about the responsibility for education in this country, and I should like to take a few minutes to point out in what ways the various jurisdictions enter into the picture. One often hears it said that the federal government of the United States does more for education than does the federal government of this country. This only serves to show up the peculiar nature of Canada, and why a policy that can be followed in the United States cannot necessarily be followed in this country. By the Quebec Act the French speaking population of Canada received certain rights. One of those rights was complete control over the education of their children. This clause was enshrined in the British North America Act, and the federal government must be very careful that its jurisdiction does not impinge on provincial jurisdiction in matters of general education.

I have cited the case of the province of Quebec, but I think I could mention any other province. I feel sure that in my own province of Ontario the provincial authorities would be very much upset, and would quickly object, if it were seen that there was any alleged interference with this exclusive provincial jurisdiction. As a result, Mr. Speaker, we may rule out the possibility of federal assistance to education on a general scale. However, there are certain special fields

than one-tenth of the provincial expenditures on roads. It is my impression that provincial governments are doing more this year. Surely it is incumbent upon this parliament within its limited function-but a very important function, I submit, Mr. Speaker- to revise drastically upwards by one means or another our assistance to universities, and particularly our assistance in the line of bursaries and scholarships.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in French to my French-speaking fellow citizens and particularly to those of my colleagues who represent Quebec constituencies.
I would ask them to support this resolution of mine because I sincerely think that it is one of the best means of promoting national unity in Canada.

Before introducing and explaining my resolution, I want to make it clear that I am among those who recognize that the provinces have competent jurisdiction in the field of education. That is the case in the province of Ontario as well as in all the provinces which stand guard jealously over their rights in the field of education.

I know that French Canadians are proud of their language, their customs and their traditions. They are right in feeling as they do, and I congratulate them on that score. In order to maintain this character, French Canadians mean to keep control of education, in so far as it concerns them. I recognize that fact, as indeed my resolution shows. I am also convinced that most Canadians, French and English speaking, recognize it too.
I am looking forward to a better future when we shall have an active exchange of students, students who will think first and foremost as Canadians.

1881368,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.5.1.4,1957-01-24,d3117809-e7d1-45d2-9762-d1a2621aa271,ca.m.3975,Mr. Michener:,,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,I would like to say how interesting I found the remarks of the hon. member for York Centre on his second presentation of this motion. It is a subject of great current interest. In fact, if a member had come into the house during the hon. gentleman's speech without having heard the order called he might have been in some doubt as to which order on the order paper

was under discussion, because we had the experience a day or two ago of hearing the Prime Minister indicate that a council would be set up and that it was the intention of the government to ask parliament for $50 million as an endowment for that council, largely for the purpose of establishing scholarships.

It is perhaps a matter of judgment, Mr. Speaker, as to whether one should address one's remarks to this subject at this time or wait for the other debate which is indicated on the order paper. I have been in some doubt on that subject. It is a question of which is the cart and which is the horse in this case. Perhaps one might say, as the hon. member for York Centre has priority in time, that at least if the government is the cart it is a pushcart being pushed by its backbenchers in this case. The lead has not come from the front.
This motion is qualified by three very interesting words which appear at the end, and I shall read the last line:
... in so far as the subject matter of this resolution is within the competence of parliament.

I propose to speak briefly on this subject under three headings. The first is the general need of scholarships for university students; second, the capacity of the federal government to provide funds for such purposes; third, I propose to deal with the question of the competence of parliament which is implicit in the motion itself.

Concerning the question of need, I think every hon. member of this house has a fair appreciation of the needs of the Canadian universities. They have been the subject of a great deal of discussion in the press and of many conferences in the least year or two, and on many occasions they have been the subject of discussions in this house. So there can foe no doubt in the minds of hon. members of this house concerning the needs of Canadian universities if they are to fulfil their function in the years ahead. We are in a forecasting mood these days. We have been looking ahead; we see the possibility of a great increase in the number of students attending universities and are aware of the needs of the universities in expanding their facilities. This resolution, however, primarily directs itself to the needs of the students themselves.

I think it would be a contribution to the debate if I called your attention, Mr. Speaker, to a paper which was delivered in this city a few months ago at the national conference of Canadian universities called on the subject of Canada's crisis in higher education. One paper was delivered by Dr. R. W. B. Jackson and Dr. W. G. Fleming, both of the department of national research of the
Ontario College of Education. The subject of the paper was ""Who goes to university?"". On page two these gentlemen posed the problem in the following terms:

The question ""Who should go to university?"" implies an unrealized ideal-a discrepancy between what should be and what is. For just as it is obvious that our universities come very far from attracting and retaining all the young people with aptitudes, interests, and traits of character needed to profit from a university education, it is equally apparent that many of those now enrolled in our universities lack the qualifications for success. The failure rates now prevailing-30 per cent is common-are intolerable even in an economy as wealthy as ours.

Following considerable discussion of the subject they arrived at conclusions which are far from satisfactory, but perhaps they are the best that could be given from the knowledge which is available. This is the first conclusion recorded on page 25:
... we may summarize the findings about ""Who Goes to University"" in this way. We really know appallingly little about our university students, in general or in particular.
I think that is a rather grave admission in these times of attempts to deal rationally with and make adequate plans for the future. The second conclusion is as follows:

The little we do know all points to the inescapable conclusion that we are extremely wasteful of our limited resources of human talent; we may be utilizing little more than one-quarter, perhaps at most one-third, of the talents of our gifted young men and women.
To my mind that is another extremely serious statement. The third conclusion reads:
We must secure more information before we can do any sensible planning, and we must be prepared to pay the cost in time, effort, and money.
This section of the paper concludes:

Finally, if we are short of trained personnel, it is our own fault. The intellectual and other abilities are present in sufficient quantity in every generation; we not only fail to use them, we fail even to recognize them.

There, I think, is the justification of the need for more scholarships on a broad basis in Canada to make use of the available abilities of this generation which, as indicated in the statement I read, are not being given the opportunities and advantages which with our democratic philosophy and ideals we recognize as the right of every citizen in equal measure. It is the democratic ideal, which we have demonstrated in elementary education, to give equal opportunity to all students. In fact it has been made compulsory for students to attend school to an age which almost completes high school education. That principle of equality which is the background of our political system, and our concept of freedom and government should also extend to university education.
Opportunity should be made available along the lines I have indicated.

The next question is, what are the needs of the students themselves? We have had some very interesting help on this subject. All hon. members have received the brief to which my hon. friend referred, presented by the national federation of Canadian university students. The one I hold in my hand is dated January 25, 1956. It is now a year old, but it shows very careful consideration by the people who ought to know of what it costs to attend university and what the prospects are for a young man or woman who is not fortunate enough to have family backing which will assure him the means to complete a year or two or three of higher education.

This document, signed by Mr. Peter G. Martin and Mr. Harry Arthurs, may have been brought up to date, but it is a clear indication from the students that it is not now possible with the current costs of university education for an ordinary person to earn and pay his own way through university. Certainly some will do it. I recall very well that when I was attending the University of Alberta there was a young man in attendance who was the envy of us all. He was an enterprising sort of fellow who went out selling Wearever aluminum products in the summer and always came back with $1,000 or $1,500 in cash which was more than he needed in those days to pay his tuition and expenses for a year at the university.

The best evidence we have today is that on the average the student who works to good advantage during the summer will make $600 net and will return to university with that sum, which he can put toward his costs; but it does not begin to cover the entire expense. The average cost of a year at university is $1,200, and that ranges from $900 in some of the smaller colleges to $1,400 at McGill. Depending on private support as it does, McGill has, I think, higher tuition fees than most universities. The student who averages $600 net has a shortage of approximately $600. Although one might say to a student, ""You are an enterprising young man in a country of vast opportunity. You can make your own way through and if necessary stay at work for a year and save enough to go to university for three years in succession,"" it does not work out that way in practice.

The challenge to make the best use of the abilities of our young people is a grave one. I agree completely with the proposition that in Canada we should have scholarships based on ability, which will ensure that all young men and women who have the capacity
for higher education shall have an opportunity to obtain it. I could cite many other documents in support of the proposition, but I think it is generally accepted.

The next point is the capacity of the federal government to provide funds for a comprehensive system of scholarships. University students in their federation asked for 2,500 annual awards, each tenable for four years, at a cost of approximately $5.5 million a year, a very modest beginning. The scope of scholarships which exist today is substantially in excess of that figure, and we are now setting aside a substantial sum of money, though not large within the figures with which the federal government deals. There is no question when one considers the real taxation, the amount of money which our expanding economy produces, and the surplus which is produced by the taxation level maintained by this parliament and this government, that the sums are available.

This year the estimates which have just been tabled called for an expenditure of $5 billion, more than was ever spent in one year except in the year of highest expenditure during the war, 1943-44, when the estimates ran to something like $5,400 million. That is a sum which I think we will be asked to exceed this year when all the supplementary estimates are in. I dare say the Minister of Finance will undertake to find that sum on a balanced basis. There is no question of the capacity of the federal treasury to meet these educational demands.

The further point which I wish to make is that which the hon. member raises in his motion, the competence of the federal authority to enter into this field. Of course that is a serious question. The basic document is the British North America Act. In section 91 it deals with the matters under federal jurisdiction. Section 91 does not mention education. The nearest approach to it is the section dealing with the establishment of penitentiaries, which has nothing remotely to do with education. Then in section 92 the exclusive powers of the provincial legislatures are dealt with. Education is not there, for the simple reason that education was so definitely a matter of provincial concern and so jealously guarded by the provinces which entered into confederation that they made a special section 93 for education which says:
In and for each province the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education . . .

Then there are some provisos which do not affect the argument which I wish to make on that point. There is the scheme of confederation. It has been recognized. I see an instance of it right here in the letter which has been
submitted to the members. The Canadian school trustees' association wrote to all members of parliament in April, 1956, and I shall read one sentence of their letter, as follows:

This year a delegation proposed to present a brief to the cabinet based on that report. Unfortunately the Prime Minister has declined to receive the delegation as he contends that education is a provincial matter.

I propose to present a question to the house. How can this need be filled within the concept of our confederation? I for one do not wish to shatter any of the rights of the provinces in the educational field. That was clearly written into the constitution. Those rights are very jealously prized, particularly by the province of Quebec, and certainly I believe this house should pay every respect to that feeling on the part of the provinces in their control over education.

As the hon. member for York Centre said, the government has taken a fairly active part in educational matters in the past. It is worth while to take a look at the pattern of this. First, there was support for the various scholarships with which we are all familiar. Some 55,000 veterans enjoyed federal assistance in secondary and undergraduate education. Of these, 44,000 were in the universities for more than a year, all with federal funds. That apparently was not regarded as a serious inroad into provincial jurisdiction.

Then we have the dominion-provincial vocational training scheme to which the hon. member has referred. It is interesting to note that in 1952-53 there were 6,000 trainees in the province of Quebec, 1,500 in the province of Ontario, and 1,500 in all the other provinces, making a total of 9,000 who were receiving training which must be considered as educational training at the expense of the federal treasury. But that of course was under agreement between the provinces and the federal government, voluntarily entered into; it was not unilateral action. It was in a different category than the proposals which are apparently anticipated in the establishment of the Canada Council.

Then in addition there are the scholarships granted annually by the Department of National Health and Welfare. The Department of National Defence has a good many scholarships under the defence research board. The Department of Trade and Commerce also has some, more particularly the national research council which offered in 1955-56 a total of 267 scholarships for a total of $336,000. This year there are 250 summer research scholarships of $800 each for teachers of engineering and natural science.
We have a precedent here for the expenditure of federal funds in the provision

of educational scholarships. The hon. member has not proposed any scheme, he has simply recommended that scholarships be founded. The question arises, why does not the present government make these expenditures for these scholarships by means of direct grants to the provinces without any strings attached except that they are to be grants for educational purposes? The other question is this. Could these scholarships be arranged by agreement with the provinces so as to preserve the principle which I have said we should not treat lightly?

What is the answer to the first question of why the government in its own measure, which we will be discussing presently, does not propose to provide these scholarships for the provinces by a lump sum grant for scholarship purposes, trusting the provincial governments, which are responsible to the electorate, to carry them out satisfactorily? The grants proposed are to be made to the Canada council to be set up and they are to be administered by them. Therefore an intermediary is placed between the federal treasury and the recipients of the scholarships. If the scheme of confederation is to be observed, surely these payments should be made to the provinces for the same purposes or be made under agreement with the provinces so that there is no question of federal interference in educational matters.

This is only part of what is necessary in Canada. We know that the need for scholarships is great. We also know that the needs of secondary and primary education are even greater. The problem is of such proportions that I suggest to the house that the answer to my question why the government does not authorize grants for education directly to the provincial authorities is that by doing so the federal government admits that it has been withholding from the provinces by overcentralization of revenues funds which they should have to carry out their responsibilities. It would be a clear admission if the federal government said to the provinces today: Here is $200 million for educational purposes, which you need, and gave it to them voluntarily.

A payment given voluntarily for education without any strings could not be considered a breach of the constitution but it would be an admission that the overcentralization that has continued since the provinces gave up their taxing authority under stress of war has been continued to the disadvantage of the provinces in carrying out their very essential and necessary functions.
My conclusion, Mr. Speaker, is that I support the idea of the resolution and will vote for it. However, I have very definite

reservations as to the method by which this obvious need is to be met. I have explained those reservations. I think it is the duty of the federal authority not to impinge. When there are ways in which education can be assisted from the federal treasury, if it must be so assisted, which are within the principles of division of authority and responsibility and are acceptable, then certainly we should not do these things in ways which are not acceptable to any of the provinces of Canada.

I am sorry that we are in a position where the federal treasury has all the money and the provincial treasuries are not able to meet their responsibilities. It would be simpler if they were because then those governments, responsible to the same electorates, would undertake to discharge their responsibilities. They have every bit as much appreciation of the needs of education at the primary, secondary and university levels as we in the federal field have. As I say, I am sorry that they are not in a position to do so.

We on this side of the house have urged the government to look a little more realistically at the division of taxing authority and not to be so niggardly in their dealings with the provinces. The surpluses that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) is able to produce could well be devoted to giving the provinces an area in which they could raise educational funds. But in the circumstances that exist, and that is what we must look at because these things are urgent, I agree that as the money is here and the need is there it is only logical that they should be brought together. The reservation I have is as to the method.

SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) upon the introduction of the resolution now before the house. I believe that last year the hon. member introduced a similar resolution and I was pleased to notice that it received widespread support from both sides of the house. While I have not had time to prepare adequately the reasons why I am very much in favour of the resolution, nevertheless I should like to take this opportunity of making a brief statement endorsing the resolution wholeheartedly.

It is needless to point out that under our constitution the field of education is a matter which comes within the exclusive jurisdiction of the legislatures of the provinces. In view of this, I am glad to note that the resolution is worded in such a manner that the legislation asked for is only such as will be within the competence of parliament.
The resolution asks that the government consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide national scholarships and bursaries for students at the university level.

Although I do not pose as a constitutional lawyer, I can see nothing wrong in a constitutional way with this parliament voting to enact legislation providing for national scholarships; nor can I see any threat to the constitution or any invasion of provincial rights by the government instituting legislation of this kind.

I was very interested in the remarks just made by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener). With much of his speech I am in agreement but I cannot agree with him when he is fearful of an invasion of provincial rights in a matter of this kind. While I do not believe in handouts by governments and in making it too easy for the youth of our nation to find their way in the world, I nonetheless support the resolution wholeheartedly and without qualification. I believe it to be only right that the government of Canada and parliament should endeavour at all times to create the widest possible opportunities for the young people of Canada. I further believe it to be a principle of good government and a principle of Liberalism to provide as nearly as possible an equality of opportunity in the realm of higher education. If equality of opportunity across the nation is to be a watchword and a principle to guide us, then by all means the federal government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide for national scholarships and bursaries.

There is no need for me, Mr. Speaker, to outline the lack of professionally trained personnel in Canada. I believe that every member of the house knows that our resources of adequately trained people are very much limited. Professionally trained personnel are not available in sufficient numbers and our shortage of mechanical and electrical engineers is something that is constituting somewhat of a threat to the development and growth of Canada. Our shortage of qualified teachers and our shortage of doctors and dentists are also things which are quite obvious to all of us.

What concerns me is that the average working man and woman in Canada is really unable to provide his or her children with a university education, despite the fact that these children are able to earn a considerable amount of money during summer vacations at jobs of their own and thus to help themselves as much as possible. A system of national
scholarships and busaries would, in my opinion, greatly aid in overcoming this state of affairs.

I believe, without hesitation, that every young person who has the capacity and the desire to train himself for one of the professions which I have already mentioned, or indeed for anything requiring higher education, should be able to do so regardless of his or her means. If any such person is prevented from doing this solely because of lack of financial resources, I believe it is a tragedy for Canada and that we should do our best to remedy such a situation.

Mr. Speaker, on numerous occasions I have put my views on record with respect to this matter, but I believe this is the first opportunity I have had in this house to do so. I cannot but call to mind a certain family whom I know in the city of Brantford. The son is a medical student at a great Canadian university. His father is a working man and is really not able to afford to maintain him there. The son works and earns money during the summer months and on every other possible occasion, in order to assist in paying for his education. The mother has gone out and has done char work. She is employed in cleaning several business establishments and several law offices in Brantford. Her husband helps her. All of the money they earn and all the money that their son earns during the summer recess- indeed all the money that they can put together from mortgaging their house and other means-is used to educate the young man at the university, and an extremely brilliant student he is. These heroic sacrifices are being made in my community and in many others in order that some of our young people can take the place in life that they desire to take.

I have in my hand, Mr. Speaker, a brief to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects submitted by the national scholarship committee of the national committee of Canadian university students. On page 11 of this brief there is a quotation from Dr. F. Cyril James, principal and vice-chancellor of McGill university:
A young Canadian from a family of modest circumstances has less chance of getting a university education today than a youth in any other country with which I am familiar.

I wonder if this statement could be true. If it is true, I think it is up to us who sit in this chamber to do something about it. Nevertheless, one thing is clear and that is that there are not enough opportunities to obtain a university education in Canada. I am told that only 4 per cent of those who start the first grade in Canadian public

schools ever graduate from university. The brief of which I have spoken also points out that as many as 54 per cent of those who abandon education at any stage do so for financial reasons. The brief asks for the institution of bursaries and scholarships in the form of awards of $2,500 tenable for four years so that a total of about 10,000 Canadian students would benefit in each year in the amount of about $500.

For the reasons I have given and in order to create more nearly equal opportunities for the youth of Canada of whom all members of parliament, I know, are proud, I feel that I must support this resolution. If I recollect correctly, I read somewhere quite recently that all the money spent by the government in providing educational facilities for veterans in the last great war has been paid back by the recipients in income taxes. That is something that may or may not be true but it is something to keep in mind while discussing this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot add anything more to what I have said. I have made only a few brief remarks and I do not think I need to say any more. I should certainly be pleased to see this matter given full and careful consideration by the government.

1881370,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.5.1.6,1957-01-24,f2bbf383-7eb4-4502-a636-9fe5ed8129ea,ca.m.5171,Mr. R. R. Knight (Saskatoon):,,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,Mr. Speaker, it is only with the greatest reluctance that I repeat myself although I know there is a psychological principle involved, namely that repetition finally has some effect. Of course, much depends upon the type of audience you have. I am not suggesting that the members of this house are such an audience but I may say that there are in this country people who need to be told over and over again about the values and the importance of education to Canada.

I said that I did not want to repeat myself. I have just discovered that on January 26, 1956 I spoke at great length on this particular situation. Today I do not propose to go into any detail of statistics or of methods but I think that I can add a word or two to what I have said previously about the general principle of the resolution. I am prepared to take the sponsor's word for it that, when he talks about these scholarships, he has in mind both graduate and undergraduate scholarships.

When I heard that this resolution was up for consideration today, I had some doubt in my mind that it would be accepted as being in order. I am glad that it has been so accepted. Of course, the fact is that legislation has already been foreshadowed-and it will be discussed in this house-which will provide the necessary machinery and arrangements by which these scholarships will be granted.

The government, in the terms of the resolution, has considered the advisability of introducing such a resolution. I am glad that the consideration of such has been fruitful. If I may I should like to quote from page 579 of Hansard of January 26, 1956, where I am reported as saying as follows:

I say I am glad that a member who supports the government brought in the resolution. I honour him for it and I wish him luck with it. It may be a good sign. Let us hope it is of some significance. Let us hope that something will be done.
Well, something is going to be done. There is no one in this house more happy about that than I am.

If I might digress for a moment from my general topic I would say that I think these private members' resolutions, irrespective of what side of the house they come from, are of inestimable value. After all, legislation is often based upon public opinion. If by means of a private member's resolution any idea of importance to this nation may be publicized and popularized throughout the country, then I am all for it. I think my friends on the other side are coming along in matters of education. I know that is not fair to some of them because some of them have come along just as far as I have, indeed farther, over the years. But I cannot help recalling the first time that I introduced a resolution in this house concerning federal aid to education. I was met with raised eyebrows and with wonder. They stood aghast that such a thing should be mentioned in the federal house. Is this, they said, not a matter completely within the jurisdiction of the provinces? My answer, of course, was yes. No one could agree more that matters of administration, matters of the choice of curricula for education are the concern only of the provinces. But I shall have a word to say about that later.

In the meantime the government has brought into this house a resolution preceding legislation which when passed, and I am sure it will be, will set up the machinery to do the very thing for which this notice of motion asks. It is true that it is couched in the devious language which convention dictates and the necessity for which must be a mystery to the average layman. We now wait that legislation, and we await it with interest and, so far as I am concerned, with joy.

Nevertheless, since this resolution has been introduced today I want to assure my hon. friend of my complete and whole-hearted support for his thesis. As I say, since legislation will come, and since there will be an opportunity at that time to discuss it, I am not going to discuss that legislation in its

detail now. I, personally, would interpret such a discussion as being out of order. It is, as I said, a source of great satisfaction to me that the people of this country at long last, and finally those in this house, have shown some concern about the educational facilities of our country.

I have talked about these private members' resolutions. I say my Liberal friends may have come along in their thinking on this subject. A moment ago I forgot to mention that when I brought in either the first or the second such resolution, one of my friends, who sits opposite to me, and who happens to be a neighbour of mine from a geographical point of view, was kind enough to say that any private member introducing a private member's resolution on this subject was doing so for political purposes and that I, personally, was bringing this one in with the deliberate intention of deceiving the public. I do not know whether the same hon. friend over there would like to make the same accusation against the hon. member who introduced this resolution. I am quite sure his colleague would not now, and I emphasize the word ""now"", make such an accusation, I venture to say, even against me. So, as I say, we are getting along a bit.

Lately there has been a great recognition that this sort of thing is constitutional. I will not go into the arguments advanced by my hon. friend the member for St. Paul's a moment ago, but I agree with them to a large extent. As I say, no one agrees more than do I that these vital things, that the program of education in each particular province, must be the sole prerogative of the people inside that province. But why in the world, if that province has not the financial resources to give the children within that province an equal opportunity of education with the children in other provinces, should we not be allowed to assist them in promoting the type of education that they, not the federal government, want to see tried. I said something the other day to the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) about that lacuna, that void, which will exist in the system of education even after this legislation has been passed. I shall not repeat it here. We shall have the opportunity to do that on another resolution which follows closely in the wake of this one.

We should consider this, that the results of such education, its efficiency and its scope, have a tremendous effect not only upon the provinces but upon the nation as a whole. In these days of fast transportation people are not stuck in any particular province. They are travelling all over the country and they are having an influence upon the whole of the

country. Think of the educationists in the province of Nova Scotia who have been so famous in that they have disseminated education of a high quality throughout the country. In the early pioneering days of the west our professors came from that multiuniversity province which is penalized today by that very efficiency and that very demand for education because of the method by which the university grants are distributed, namely the per capita method. We find such a percentage demand for university education in Nova Scotia that that ultimately reduces the amount per student almost to half what it is in some other provinces.

May I say this province has schools of a type that are not available in the other provinces, professional schools if you like to call them, and I think there are none of those, for example, in the province of Newfoundland. You get an influx, therefore, from the other provinces into Nova Scotia with the result that Nova Scotia is penalized in regard to the amount of the grant per student attending their schools of higher learning.

I was saying that provincial education, no matter what type it is, must be a type prescribed by the people themselves, and that the province-this is the repetition, Mr. Speaker, in which I have been saying it is necessary to indulge-let me say that the whole nation is affected by the efficiency of the education in each one of these provinces. We have come to the conclusion that we must develop our human resources just as we have the inclination-perhaps not from as good a motive-to develop our natural heritage. These human resources are those fine young men and women who are your children and mine. We have come to recognize that if we are to develop to the full extent our natural heritage and to develop it for the good of future generations, then amongst this still small population of ours there must be the leaven or the yeast of developed minds.

Our urge toward this end has been stimulated-and I do not think it is the best of motives-by the rivalry of the example of others. I need not point out to you the magnitude of the efforts in regard to scholarships that have been made by certain eastern European countries with whose ideologies we do not agree and who are anxious to prove that their whole system is superior to ours. I remember quoting last year a startling statement by Mr. Burke Stannard-perhaps I can find it. Incidentally, he may be surprised to know, if he does me the honour to read this speech, that I knew him very well as a little boy. He made this statement in that startling argument:
In 1918, Russia had one university for every 1.5 million population; Canada had one for every
315,000. Today, Russia has one university student for every 150 population; Canada has one for every 250.
Mr. Stannard's article was published in the Financial Post on December 18, 1954. This is the situation we find in our country of Canada which calls itself progressive.

Well, I said those nations, and particularly Russia, have a great system of scholarships, much greater than any foreshadowed in any legislation that is for the moment proposed here. Yes, and some friendly nations, too, whose ideas in general are akin to our own, have left us far behind in this particular matter. Seventy-five per cent-I think this figure has been bandied about; the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) may not endorse the figure for he insists it is 74 per cent, but we shall let it go for the moment- seventy-five per cent of all students attending British universities do so with government assistance of some kind or other, and the majority of that assistance is in the form of scholarships. It is equally true that 70 per cent of all the expenditure of universities in the British Isles is provided by the state. Having in mind the success of their system, I would urge that the scholarships advocated here be granted
and note this carefully because I think it is important-be granted upon the basis of need plus ability, not on the basis of need, not on the basis of ability, but on the basis of need plus ability.

I was intrigued a bit by the last speaker, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown), who quite unconsciously used the term ""the working man"". You could see back of his thinking there is the tradition that because a man's father is a working man he has no chance to go through university. He cannot go to university perchance because his father worked. Well, there is a big principle, a big idea behind that. We are changing all that now. ""Nous avons change tout cela"", said Moliere in the play ""Le m6decin malgre lui"". It will change more and never again will it be part of our language to say that a boy did not go to school, he did not go to university because his father was a working man. Those who are philosophers might think that over. There must, of course, be no distinction in regard to the stratum or the position that students occupy in society, in the granting of assistance to them. Hon. members would expect that remark to come from me. The finest brains are not necessarily found in any stratum of society.

It is most important that students of ability, whose parents could never hope to send them to university or to maintain them at a university, should have the opportunity to attend. Nowadays ability to learn and aptitude

for learning are easily discoverable by scientific methods quite early in life. Clever and hard-working students are recognized under the British system by their methods there, and once recognized are encouraged toward further advance by a system of what is called ""free places"" in higher schools, and are the recipients of the scholarships such as are envisaged by my hon. friend. In Britain students are often chosen by competitive examination. Thus the best brains of the country are retained in the service of the nation and in the service of their fellow men.

When I was talking a little while ago about the educational results in the provinces I was thinking of a Quebecois, or a man from Saskatchewan or from Manitoba or British Columbia. He gets his education here or there but he is fundamentally a Canadian, and by his ability is the country of Canada judged.

I do not know enough about the British system, either of its merits or of its demerits, if it has any of the latter, to debate it in detail here, but I would urge those who are responsible for the award of those scholarships which are envisaged here to examine the machinery I have described, when they are setting up the system of scholarship awards in Canada.

I am glad, sir, that it appears in the projected giving of scholarships some attention will be paid to the humanities. When I say ""attention"" I mean extra attention. In the past there has been a tendency to favour the sciences, and that tendency perhaps has been natural enough in a country that has found it necessary to develop defence programs where men of science are in particular demand. It is natural, too, in a country which has set out to develop its great natural resources. I have no quarrel with scholarships in the scientific field; in fact I would urge an increase. But I think there should be a balance. Scholarships are scanty enough in our country, goodness knows, and I look with pleasure upon their being increased no matter for what educational purpose, but I think we should have that balance.

Let me say categorically it is my belief there is no better basis for an education, even for those who are later going to enter the field of specialization, than a broad grounding in the humanities, known sometimes, Mr. Speaker, as a liberal education. With this increase in national scholarships there will be a corresponding need for assistance to universities in order that those universities shall be able to provide the increased facilities which will come from increased enrolment owing to the scholarships.
I need not explain to this house that I have always pleaded for greater equality of

opportunity in education. I must confess that for the most part my thinking did relate largely to the primary and secondary schools. Such equality of opportunity could extend- nay, would extend-to all those who are attending school. If all children had that opportunity it would extend to all the mass of secondary students who would be available for the granting of the scholarships envisaged in this resolution.

Although I could have made a better case today by quoting a great many authorities on education, of which I am not one, I have up to this point expressed my own thoughts. After I had already made up my mind what I might say this afternoon there came into my hands a brochure which I would recommend that all hon. members of this house read. The documented arguments for the granting of university scholarships have been presented in a masterly and convincing fashion in this little booklet by experts in the field of education. The booklet is entitled, ""The university teacher and the crisis of higher education in Canada,"" and it was presented as a brief to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects by the Canadian Association of University Teachers. I am going to follow my announced intention not to quote from the authorities this afternoon but I would hope that the people in this house who are interested in this subject would read the arguments and recommendations contained in this brief. I have perhaps a particular interest in its because the chairman of the association which issued this report is Dr. V. C. Fowke who is a professor of economics at the University of Saskatchewan situated in my own constituency of Saskatoon. My purpose in mentioning the booklet is simply to recommend a study of it to all those who are interested.

I am well aware that in the matter of intelligence Providence has not distributed its bounty with an even hand. I am also well aware that there are many whose capabilities do not lie in the direction of higher education but who nevertheless make a very successful and happy life in other fields. As one who has struggled with high school students for a part of his life at least I am also well aware that there are those who are not prepared to do the work necessary for the attainment of higher education and sometimes for the attainment of even an elementary education. One has to come to a decision here, but putting these things together let me say at once that I am not prepared to ask the nation to subsidize the cost of attendance at schools of higher learning of those who either cannot or will not put forth the necessary

effort to take advantage of such an opportunity when it is presented to them. But concerning those who have the ability, that is an entirely different matter. To those who have any marked degree of capacity to learn combined with a willingness to work, let us be generous. Let us be generous almost to a fault, not just for their own sakes, but for the benefit of future generations, and for the benefit of a future Canada which they will make great in proportion to how well they are equipped to create it.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Robert Ross (Roy) Knight,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=f2bbf383-7eb4-4502-a636-9fe5ed8129ea&Language=E&Section=ALL
1881371,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.5.1.7,1957-01-24,9489ab9c-9ef3-40d5-813a-6bf676f6dcaf,ca.m.4895,Mr. H. M. Batten (Humber-St. George's):,,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,It is with much pleasure that I support the resolution on scholarships introduced in the house on January 26 of the last regular session and reintroduced today by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Holling-worth). I would also commend him for his efforts in presenting this resolution at a time when all across this country there is a growing interest in the need for and the needs of education, at a time when more than a little cohcern is being expressed by those whose duty and responsibility it is to administer systems and institutions of learning so essential to the progress of this country, at a time when those who have need for trained personnel are finding that the supply in many fields is far too short. Many have expressed quiet concern while others have been more pronounced in their opinions as to the current problems in education as well as the difficulties which will need attention in the immediate future both at the high school, technical school and university levels.

Within recent months there has been great emphasis placed on the need for more graduates in the professional fields. I do not believe that the position has been overstated. The need is great and I suspect that it will be so for some time. Indeed it may be a good omen that our economy has so expanded as to demand such large numbers of technical and professional graduates, but at the same time it must be admitted that such a demand may not be an indication of strength if the facilities for supplying that demand are not present, or not capable of being provided.

But while we do live in an economy where vocational training and professional faculties are vital and essential, and while we know that these faculties will have to be expanded to meet our growing technical needs, we must remember that something more than the practical must be taught if higher education is to make the contribution which a democracy such as Canada will demand of it. I am not trying to lessen the importance of the need nor the value of the science courses when I say that we could take all the

science courses out of our universities and there would still be a place for the university in Canadian society. Education is not only a preparation for making a living, but also for living a life. We must be careful not to introduce economic conscription into our educational system at the expense of the real meaning and the real need for education in its broader sense. This is one of the reasons why I welcomed the resolution dealing with the Canada Council and aid to universities introduced by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a few days ago.

We live in a land which over a period of a few years has become industrialized to a comparatively high level. Today there is need for more trained personnel in nearly every field. Without doubt this is true in the various fields of applied science and in all those where technical knowledge is essential. Dr. O. M. Solandt, former president of the defence research board, in speaking to the Canadian Industrial Preparedness Association two years ago said:

If we are to remain free we must contribute more and more to the scientific advances of the free world; if we are to remain prosperous we must do the research and development that will enable us to produce more and better goods more cheaply in order to compete effectively in world markets.
This statement coming from such a prominent Canadian scientist merits the attention of all Canadians who attempt to envisage the possibilities and potentialities of this great land.

In the development of the material side of our economy, the individual and his development must not be obscured. It has been said that the wealth of a nation depends upon production and that in turn production depends upon the available quantity of different raw materials plus the labour involved in producing goods for which there are profitable markets. I suppose all of us would agree that this is not a complete definition of national wealth, but in whatever definition modern economists might give for national wealth, materials and labour would be prominent. These two must go together if there is to be production. It might well be said that these two are so interdependent upon each other that they are of equal importance and yet I believe that in a land where there is a high potential source of labour and a high potential source of material, the source of labour, whether that labour be unskilled, semi-skilled, skilled or professional, must have precedence for its existence and for its improvement.
I should like to quote Protagoras, that great Greek philosopher of the third century B.C., and an older contemporary of Socrates.

I quote him for two reasons; first, because the statement which I want' to use is attributed to him, and second, because in a discussion on the present means of education it may be appropriate to quote the man who is recorded by history as being the first to teach for payment. Protagoras said:
Man is the measure of all things.

One of the problems of our time is to reconcile the dignity of man with the technical achievements of modern society. The real measure of a modern industry is its power to preserve our human values while adding to our material heritage. We must remember that man is not just another link in the productive chain, he is the very reason for its existence.

In this day it might be well to ponder why it is that such large sums of money are spent to refine our natural resources by government and industry when so much of the attempt to improve our human resources is left to individual effort. So I would like to have as a characteristic of any scholarship program which may be in existence now or which may come into being as a result of this or any other resolution, equality of opportunity for assistance in the arts and humanities as well as in the sciences.

May I turn now to another phase of this problem. Generally Canadians are aware that under the British North America Act education is essentially the responsibility of the provinces. I believe it was a wise decision then and I consider it to be a wise decision today, almost a century later. I do not think that a centrally controlled system of education would be a good thing for a country like Canada. However, this is not the time to discuss the merits or demerits of such a system. Suffice it to say that while I believe that the practice of education should be within the jurisdiction of the provinces, I also believe that as our national life becomes more complex, as our interprovincial relations and dependencies lead us toward a unity in multiplicity, and as provincial standards in any phase of living must have an effect on similar standards for the nation as a whole so a responsibility which is essentially provincial may have a national aspect which will demand attention.

At this time I do not propose to project this argument beyond the limitations of the present resolution. I think that such scholarships as this resolution envisages would do much to offer encouragement to those who are handicapped by conditions of geography and finance, to decrease our losses in wasted brain power, and to conserve and develop those human resources of talent and ability which Canada will need in the years which

lie ahead. And so the second characteristic of the program suggested by this resolution that I would welcome would be that such scholarships be open to students from all regions of Canada and that they be tenable at any Canadian university, always provided that the student is able to satisfy the entrance requirements of the university of his choice.

In a scholarship program I should also like to see provision made for those who pursue education courses at university or in teacher training institutions. I know that in all provinces efforts are being made to attract young men and women into the teaching profession, and while there are other important factors affecting the low rate of recruitment, encouragement should be given where possible. The teaching profession must not only perpetuate itself by preparing those who will later enter the profession, but must prepare those who will go on to study in other fields in our higher institutions of learning. I believe that a successful effort to place within the day schools of this country teachers who are qualified will do much to decrease the tremendous waste indicated by the large numbers who fail to reach the standard during the first year of university.

In many provinces of Canada there is a desperate need for qualified teachers. It is noteworthy that while many university faculties have been overcrowded teacher training institutions have been operating with less than the numbers which they could normally accommodate. In 1953 there were 142 institutions in Canada for the training of teachers. The reported enrolment capacity was 16,260 while the actual enrolment was 12,424. In other words, at a time when the demands for recruitment to the teaching profession is urgent, our teacher training institutions are operating at 76 per cent capacity. In the Atlantic provinces these institutions operated at 57 per cent of the possible total enrolment.

In my own province of Newfoundland the shortage of teachers is something more than serious; it is critical and alarming. There are not nearly enough trained people to staff our schools and even after employing those who are not qualified there are still schools, particularly in the outlying areas, where no teacher supply has been possible. The situation would be further aggravated if the teacher load were reduced to thirty pupils per teacher.

On Wednesday of last week a conference was called in St. John's to discuss the various phases of this problem in a very serious minded manner. Public concern was well emphasized by the presence at that conference of many who, although not directly

engaged in the field of education, recognize that in the regional development of our province education must play an important role. Regardless of statements that we have heard floating around about the maritimes in the last few days, we in Newfoundland have been there for over 460 years and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we will be there for a long time yet. But if Newfoundland is to occupy the place in the Canadian federation which I think it is capable of occupying we will need to develop not only the natural resources of the area but also the human resources by providing schools that will develop independent thinking based on knowledge of the past, understanding of the present and good judgment about the future. To do this we will need not only the encouragement and assistance of scholarship programs, the Canada Council, university aid and vocational training but also the assistance of any other sources which may be available to us.

In recent months there has been evidenced a great deal of interest in the progress being made in other countries in education, particularly in the different fields of applied science. There is very little need to repeat here statistics dealing with university enrolment in other countries. They have already been presented to the house over the past few months. It is a good thing that we know what others are doing and I think it is important that we should know what others are doing but I suggest that the really important comparison is not to compare what Canada is doing now with what other countries are doing but to compare what we are doing now with what we need to do in this country to satisfy our requirements for national defence, to maintain our position in the community of nations, and for the development of our own country to the limits of which it is capable.

A comparatively new word has come into the English language, Mr. Speaker, that word being automation. I suppose we could define it as the process in industry by which production is operated, regulated and continued automatically. In a country such as Canada, with its present industrial development and its future potential, one would expect that we should look forward and anticipate the advantages which automation has to offer. Some fear that such a process will result in further unemployment. I do not believe that such need be the case. True it is that there may be less demand for unskilled labour but I believe there will be many more opportunities for better employment available to those who are qualified to take them.

The efforts of the provinces and the federal government under the Vocational Training Co-ordination Act, which has been in effect for the last 18 years, have been commendable. The continuation and extension of the schedule will not only do much to provide the many technicians Canada will need in the years that lie ahead but will do much to eliminate the waste in that segment of our youth who have the ability to engage in technical pursuits but are hindered by financial or other reasons from acquiring those skills which industry will demand of them.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, may I say again that I support the purpose of the resolution as I would support the purpose of any resolution tending toward the fuller development of the mental, physical and spiritual values of the people of the country, for I believe that it is by such development that we will be able to produce Canadians who are strong and sound individuals and at the same time individuals who are sound and strong Canadians. I believe that it is by such development that Canada will be able to produce that type of Canadian who will work more effectively in the society in which he lives and at the same time live more abundantly in the society in which he works.

,Liberal,,Herman Maxwell Batten,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=9489ab9c-9ef3-40d5-813a-6bf676f6dcaf&Language=E&Section=ALL
