SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be able to take part this afternoon in a debate on such a worthy resolution as the one now before us which the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) saw fit to present to the house again this year. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by former speakers in the debate, and with many of the arguments advanced in support of the resolution I agree entirely. However, I was particularly impressed with one reservation respecting the resolution advanced by the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener), and I must say that I think the particular reservation he made in his speech is one worthy of great concern.

I wish to commend also the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) for again speaking at such great length on a problem which has for years been very close to his heart. We look upon the resolution as one actually twofold in its purpose. First, it proposes to enable university students now in attendance at universities across Canada and who find themselves unable to continue their studies because of a shortage of funds to be able to continue. Second, it proposes to provide funds which will be used for worthy graduates from our secondary schools who also find themselves with insufficient funds to embark upon university studies.

The resolution is indeed pertinent at this session in view of the proposed government legislation along the same lines. For far too long we have had too many people in Canada giving pious lip service to the saying that Canada is a land of equal opportunity for all. As one travels across Canada and as one listens to the speeches delivered in the house by hon. members from various parts of the country, one cannot help but realize that Canada does not offer equal opportunities for all. This is particularly true in the field of education.

I was impressed with the remarks of one hon. member this afternoon when he pointed out that down through the years educators from the province of Nova Scotia have been leaving that province, going to other provinces of the dominion and offering their services as educators. That is quite true, and perhaps as a result education has suffered somewhat in the province of Nova Scotia. On the other hand, we in other parts of Canada have gained considerably from the talents these people have brought to other parts of the country, particularly western Canada.

The matter of scholarships and bursaries has given the government of the province of Alberta great concern over the past years. That government has already embarked upon a co-operative scheme involving the province and divisional and other school boards throughout Alberta for the purpose of giving bursaries and scholarships to graduates of our high schools in Alberta to encourage them to enter the faculty of education in our province.

The shortage of teachers throughout Canada has already been mentioned. From my own school district, a district for which I worked many years, we have in attendance in the faculty of education at Edmonton this year 16 former students. Out of this number of 16 students in the faculty of education, only one happens to be a man. I am not for one moment discounting the value of ladies in the teaching profession. However, I feel that any profession, particularly that of education, requires the help at least of a certain number of men.

I have already mentioned the bursaries and scholarships which the provincial government and the school divisions are jointly providing for graduates of our high schools in Alberta who enter the field of education. The province of Alberta a few years ago established what was known as the students assistance act. This act provides to university students scholarships which will entitle them to enter any faculty at our university. Again, our province has seen fit to establish what is

called a revolving fund. Students desiring to enter the University of Alberta can borrow from this fund an amount equal to $400 a year. This amount of $400 a year is given to the students at a low rate of interest. Since it is a revolving fund the students, upon graduation, are expected to pay the money which they borrowed from the fund back to it. The money is paid back in annual payments of $200 commencing at the end of the first complete year after graduation. I feel that we in Alberta have gone a long way towards encouraging the graduates of our high schools to enter our university. On the other hand, I recognize that limits are to be found in provincial revenue available for this purpose and that perhaps we have gone about as far as we can go. Certainly we in Alberta would readily accept the assistance of the federal government in this connection.

We are continually reminded, Mr. Speaker, in this house, through the press and over the radio that the U.S.S.R. is going all-out in the matter of encouraging the young people of that country to enter the institutions of higher learning. We are informed that this encouragement is particularly strong in the field of engineering and in other associated scientific courses. We are spending billions of dollars each year to maintain a defensive war machine to protect the free world from communist aggression. With this expenditure I have little quarrel but I do feel that we must also give increasing attention to the educational development of our young people so that we shall have in Canada an enlightened group of young people who are not only capable of matching the wits and the minds of the young people of the communist world but who are willing and able to take leadership in the establishment of a truly free world where peace and goodwill will reign eternally.

SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,Mr. Speaker, may I extend my sincere congratulations to the two members who have spoken a few words in the French language. I wish to congratulate them not in the name of the French Canadians whom I represent in the house but in the name of all Canadians in the country because the country as a whole shares in common the two precious cultures of our national character.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening attentively to the speeches which have just been delivered in support of the resolution now before the house. Though each and every one of the speakers carefully pointed out that he would favour the introduction of such legislation only in so far as it would respect provincial rights in matters of education, I must admit that, as far as I could see, they

gave no reason why we should believe that those exclusive provincial rights in the field of education could really be respected in the implementation of this resolution. Nevertheless I do want to pay tribute to its sponsor. He does indicate that he only wishes to attain his objective, as he spells out in his resolution:
... in so far as it falls within the competence of parliament.
Those words are to be found at the end of the resolution itself and may be said to provide cause for repeating the latin saying: in cauda venenum.

That condition is one of the reasons, and the main reason, so far as I am concerned, for opposing the resolution since it does not offer sufficient guarantees as to how it might be achieved without impairment of exclusive provincial jurisdiction in matters of education.

Of course each of the speakers carefully pointed out his personal desire to respect those rights. That is also, I believe, the intention of the sponsor of the resolution. Still I think that if we enter the field of education, one reserved to the provinces, we have no means of knowing what, in ten or fifteen years time, will have become of all the good intentions of those people who stated their desire to respect those rights.

Along with the hon. gentlemen who have spoken before me, I recognize the crying need which is apparent throughout our country for an increase in revenue for educational purposes. I believe that on this point even the most resolute champions of provincial rights, who deny that the federal government has any right whatever in this field, will recognize the tremendous requirements of this country with regard to education. That is no justification however for the federal government to enter the educational field.

One, or even two hon. members, one on each side of the house, advanced the argument that the whole of Canada was affected by education which is provided in any given province. Now that is one of the arguments which, to my mind, were taken from the Massey Commission Report and which have been advanced in support of the theory that universities are of general national interest, a fact which has allowed the federal government to interfere in university education as it is doing now.

Let us take the same argument, let us apply it to primary education; we will then be able to adduce the very same reasons in support of the theory that primary education has national consequences. Let us take all the fields reserved to the provinces by our constitution. It can always be claimed that
everything that a province does may have repercussions on the nation as a whole, an argument which will bring us, little by little, to the taking over of each and every provincial prerogative.

Since we are all agreed on the necessity of aiding education, why do we not return to the provinces the taxation rights which were borrowed from them, and thus enable them, according to the terms of the constitution, to meet their commitments, which they have, in fact, no thought of denying in the matter of education.

Then again, of course, it could be claimed that it is not so in the case of the poor provinces since they might not be in a position to meet their educational obligations without federal help, and because the federal government keeps those taxation fields it has borrowed in order to help those very provinces. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I am far from convinced that the rights which have not been returned to the provinces are being used solely to help the poorer provinces. I am very hopeful, along with every hon. member in this house, that the day may come when representatives of the provincial governments and of the federal government may meet around a table and settle once and for all this problem of taxation rights, which is at the basis of all problems connected with education submitted to the federal government, so that provinces may enjoy rights which are really theirs and each and everyone of them may, according to the spirit of the constitution, meet the obligations placed upon it by the constitution. It would then be possible not only to take into account the needs of the poorer provinces, but also to restore to the others those powers which are exclusively theirs according to our constitution. It would solve this recurrent problem, one that will crop up once again when we will be called upon to discuss legislation providing for university grants or the trans-Canada highway, or the Unemployment Insurance Act, where there has been federal government interference.

As long as the federal government continues to interfere in provincial matters, we will be faced with the same problem, that of the resdistribution of taxation powers. We must ensure that at each level of civil authority the proper body is in a position to meet its obligations with sufficient funds. We will then no longer see a central government plagued with a surfeit of money while those really in need of revenue are deprived of the means to meet their obligations. We will no longer hear this government say: ""Well, the state must now look after education since
the provinces are not in a position to meet the cost"" because they would have been deprived of their taxation powers.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I was a little surprised this afternoon to hear some hon. members draw comparisons with the educational system of Russia.

It might be true that in Russia more money is spent on certain forms of education than in Canada. I rather think, however, that if Canada were to resort to the same means, abolishing private enterprise and chopping off heads, etc., we might solve all our educational problems. But that is hardly a fair comparison. I do not think, in fact, that hon. members really wished to set up Russia as an example of what should be done in the educational field, because the means employed in that country are a denial of those sacred rights which we seek to promote through education.

I will now bring my remarks to a close. I shall have further opportunity to deal with this topic when we will take up the matter of university grants, one closely connected with the resolution we are discussing this afternoon.

I congratulate the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) on the spirit in which he moved his resolution, because I really believe that he sincerely wishes to bring a solution to a need which everyone recognizes but, neither in his resolution nor in the speeches made this afternoon, can I see how, in supporting his motion, we can preserve the exclusive rights of the provinces in that field.

,Independent,,Fernand Girard,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=51dde446-7fb8-4093-bc28-9fffafa7ad05&Language=E&Section=ALL
1881374,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.5.1.10,1957-01-24,d25060a9-6d52-4461-a569-fc17c9e6d009,ca.m.654,Mr. W. G. Dinsdale (Brandon-Souris):,,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,The

encouraging part of a discussion of this kind, to me, is the growing interest that is being displayed on all sides of the house in the subject of education. Very often the political pundits dwell on the notion that it takes a long time for democracy to respond to a critical situation in the body politic. I am sure it is encouraging to note that even where we have a government that is as well insulated from the impact of public opinion as is the present Canadian government, there is a gradual response to what has been described by many authorities on the subject as a crisis in education.

We have before us, under the title of ""Notices of Motion"", no less than two resolutions from private members dealing with the important subject of education. We have also a resolution from the government itself

which parallels very closely the subject matter provided for discussion by this resolution put forward by one of the back benchers supporting the government, the hon. member for York Centre. The third resolution is the regular resolution we have had on the subject of federal aid for education sponsored by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight).

It is quite obvious that there is a growing need in this country for a comprehensive examination of the problem of education in general. Not only is the interest growing in this chamber but during recent months we have had repeated representations from various educational bodies outside of this chamber. The national conference of Canadian universities has been urgent in bringing recommendations to bear upon all hon. members of parliament. The teachers' federation, in equally strong terms, makes reference to the problem. Most encouraging, however, is the new interest of leaders of industry and business in the needs of education today. Admittedly this interest arises largely from the crisis, if I may use that word again, that is occurring in connection with the shortage of technicians. Down through the years industry and business has not assisted in an overly generous way in meeting the problems of education, particularly on the higher level. In the past few months, especially last fall, they have demonstrated in no uncertain way that they regard the present situation in Canada as a real crisis. They are moving in a fairly rapid way to come to grips with the problem.

The resolution which we have before us this afternoon deals with only a small phase of the difficulty. As I read it, Mr. Speaker, it is asking the government to consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide national scholarships and bursaries for students at the university level who are in financial need. Now, that meets one small segment of the difficulty; but what we are faced with today is a crisis in education at all levels. The Canadian population is increasing and we are moving towards an industrial economy. There are very rapid changes taking place in the Canadian way of life. We are moving towards a more complex type of society. It automatically follows that new skills and new knowledge are required in order to heal the schisms that tend to flourish during a period of rapid social change and during a period of rapid movement to a more complex society.
Related to the problem of education on the university level is the problem of education on the elementary and high school level. It is quite true that a major difficulty in

the lack of sufficient recruits for our universities and colleges is the economic and financial difficulty. However, there is also the factor of lack of incentive and this is something that has to be dealt with on the lower levels of our education system, the elementary and high school levels. It is only recently that our school systems in the various provinces have introduced any form of vocational guidance program. One of the encouraging improvements in the approach to education on these lower levels, I feel, is the establishment in the province of Ontario, for example, of a separate vocational guidance program within the general public school program.

I am sure most hon. members, when they look, back on their own educational experience, will agree that it was a process of groping and hoping; it was a hit or miss approach to the selection of some vocation, and very often time and money were wasted in arriving at the final niche in which we were to pursue our life's work. That problem is being met on the elementary level. This has a very particular bearing on the new need in an industrial society for hundreds, indeed thousands, of technicians. We have methods of testing now, intelligence tests, aptitude tests, which, within reasonable limits, make it possible for a student graduating from our high school program to determine whether he would serve most usefully by taking a university course in one of the professions or by moving on to training in the technical schools. With regard to the latter, unfortunately we do not have the type of technical schools in this country that will be needed to supply the training for this type of technician qualified to do the job in a technological civilization.

While I for one welcome the resolution, may I say it deals only with a very small part of the total problem that has been thrust upon us by the very rapid changes that have taken place in Canada and in every other country of the western world in the past 10 years. It will help, but the suggestion I am putting before the house this afternoon is that the time has come in Canada when we need a co-ordinated and a comprehensive examination of the education situation that has now reached the proportions of a crisis.

There is another aspect of education that we sometimes ignore, that is just as important as the high school level or the university level. I refer to the growing significance of the adult education program in this country. Up to the present moment this work has largely been carried on, on a voluntary basis, by the Canadian Association for Adult Education, an association that has made rapid

strides in recent years, and has made a very worth-while contribution to the general solution of our educational problem. In recent years some provinces have been taking an increasing interest in this growing educational need through their adult education departments and also through their university extension departments. But here again, Mr. Speaker, is an area of education that is going to grow very rapidly in its demands with the passing years. For example, we shall be faced in the next 20 years, if we are to draw conclusions from the findings of the Gordon commission, with a work situation where we shall have decreasing hours of work and a rising standard of living. That means we shall be faced with the problem of leisure time, what to do with the leisure hours that will be at our disposal as the work week gradually decreases as the result of automation, improved productivity in the industrial process, and so forth. This increased leisure time will constitute a real educational challenge to the nation. If we use the new-found leisure time arising from an increased standard of living in a constructive, a positive and a creative way it will add immeasurably to the enrichment of the lives of Canadians. On the other hand, if we fail to meet this challenge of adult education then, of course, it will lead to a situation of frustration.

Some years ago a social scientist of some repute Thorstein Veblen wrote a book entitled, ""The Theory of the Leisure Class"". The basic thesis of his book was that it is from the leisure classes that the new ideas, the creative ideas, have emerged. Formerly, before the advent of machinery, the numbers of the leisure class were restricted to the landed aristocracy and to a very small segment of the population. Today, we are faced with a rapid expansion in that particular segment of the population. I say that is something that this parliament and all the representatives of the people, maybe more especially on the provincial level, will have to give heed to.

The criticism is often made when we discuss education in this house that we are dealing with a subject that has not much significance for a large portion of the population. The senior citizens, for example, are particularly mentioned in this regard. I would like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps the most useful part of the adult education movement has been the programs carried on among our senior citizens, the formation of second mile clubs. The idea that once a man reached the age of retirement he had nothing else to do but to retire to an institution for senior citizens and there vegetate

for the rest of his days, is a notion that is rapidly passing away. While the theory is still far too prevalent, here is a group who have enjoyed long years of life, who have acquired considerable experience during their earthly pilgrimage, who could, if the opportunity were afforded, rather than merely existing in their latter days enter into a new and a rich experience of living.

I mention this broader approach to the problem because, while we are dealing in this resolution with a very small segment of the difficulty, namely, the provision of scholarships and bursaries for students at the university level, I think that a limited program of this kind-and I am making the reservation, of course, that out of our discussion of the Canada Council and the legislation that will be forthcoming we might be dealing in a more comprehensive way with this situation -I say that our resolution merely touches the fringe of the crisis in education.

Looking at it from the standpoint of the resolution we have before us, perhaps the most beneficial use to which bursaries and scholarships can be put at this stage is in assisting in the training of teachers. Already two hon. members who have spoken in this discussion this afternoon have dealt with the teacher shortage on all levels of our educational system as a main point in their remarks. This shortage is critical at the elementary and high school levels. I do not have to dwell on that aspect of the difficulty. In all parts of Canada there is a problem of adequately staffing our schools with qualified teacher personnel. I think it was Dean Gen-dron of Ottawa University who said, in a recent discussion of this question, that in the next five years 1,124 new professors will be required in the field of pure and applied science alone. That is just one small area of the whole educational field. If we are going to begin to cope with the crisis in education the first and primary need is for an adequate number of properly trained teacher personnel.

Why is it difficult to obtain teachers? That is a big subject in itself. Certainly it is because of the problem that the resolution attempts to deal with, namely that students who would otherwise enter university in preparation for the teaching profession are unable to do so because they do not have the necessary financial wherewithal. A great many of our teachers come from the rural areas and it is in the rural areas of the country that the greatest difficulty is found in providing higher education to the young people.
Another reason is the depressed salary schedules. This subject has been discussed

recently in rather influential quarters. Mr. Muir, president of the Royal Bank of Canada, in his annual statement dealt at some length with the matter of depressed salary schedules in the teaching profession and the effect they have in discouraging the recruitment of our young people for this profession. There is the prestige factor, too. One expression comes to my mind and it has been used with sufficient frequency that it has almost become an adage: ""Those who can, do; those who cannot, teach"". It contains a derogatory implication as far as the teaching profession is concerned.

Of course we all know the story of the professor who was nicknamed ""Sanka"" by his students. This story always draws a laugh from an audience which suggests there is an underlying attitude of derogation toward the teaching profession. Perhaps I may be permitted to repeat the story. A professor was given the nickname Sanka by his students. He did not understand the meaning of the word because it was foreign to him until one day he noticed the slogan on a can of Sanka coffee which said, ""98 per cent of the energy has been removed from the bean"". That is one factor which discourages an increased interest on the part of our young people in the teaching profession.

The hon. member for Battle River-Camrose (Mr. Smith) said there is a tendency for the male of the species to shy clear of the teaching profession and I believe this is true. Perhaps one of the reasons for the continuing chronic shortage of teacher personnel is the fact that the ladies have a greater tendency to become matrimonial casualties and thus are taken out of circulation. It is not the recognized thing for men to enter the teaching profession in the numbers required to meet the demand. I could go on speaking about this particular subject at some length because I think it is one of the major problems of education today. We have a shortage of money facilities and personnel right down the line but until we have an adequately trained teacher force to deal with all the aspects of this problem then we will not be able to cope with what has been described by responsible people in all walks of life today as a crisis in education. This resolution might well be designed to encourage an increased interest in teacher training facilities and activities.

With the present trend toward bigness and centralization on all sides as we move toward a complex industrial society there is a growing tendency to neglect the smaller institutions of learning. Reference has been made
to the outstanding contributions to education which have come from our maritime provinces.

1881392,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.5.1.28,1957-01-24,d54e6b1c-79fc-4127-b9da-c703dd15e814,ca.m.4989,Mr. Cavers:,,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,I was not here that long ago so I am not able to recall that far. However, I know that he is an outstanding educationist in his part of the country. The hon. member for York Centre is a young man of outstanding attainments who comes from an area which would be expected to direct its undergraduates to one of the larger universities of Canada. But I am sure that in presenting his resolution he is motivated by the genuine desire to advance education and universities in all parts of Canada.

I feel I have a right and an obligation to speak on the resolution, the purpose of which is to provide national scholarships and bursaries at the university level for students who are in financial need. In 1930 I was one of those who had enrolled in a university course. But in that year I had the misfortune to lose my father and I had to decide whether I would continue the university course or pursue my studies in the law. I left the university at that time and continued in a legal course. Therefore I feel that from a practical standpoint I should say something on the subject.

This afternoon the hon. member for Hum-ber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) placed his finger on the principle involved in the discussion when he referred to the pith of the argument being ""equality of opportunity"". The basis of my argument is that we should make available to all young Canadian students who have the aptitude and the desire for further university training the opportunity to pursue the study of their choiee in whatever course they desire to continue, whether it be English and history, political science and economics, modern languages, the sciences, medicine, dentistry or the law.

While I speak in support of the resolution for the adoption of national scholarships and bursaries, I do not feel that we should do away with the opportunity for students to help themselves. There is a great need for students to work hard, indeed, to work very hard in order to earn the financial resources to assist in obtaining a university education. I think that not only must the

student work hard at the course of his choice in order that he may attain high standards but that it is not a bad thing that he should be required to work hard in some type of physical or business activity. The beneficial effects of part-time summer employment or work during the Christmas holidays are manifold. In my opinion the appreciation of money earned is advantageous to the student and there is the pride of achievement in having assisted oneself in one's work at the university.

We have heard today something of the obligations and problems that arise from the constitutional standpoint. Canada's federal structure has placed within the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures the right to deal with matters of education but I feel that it is rather matters of the curriculum of study and administration of schools that were meant to be under the jurisdiction of the provinces than the question of financial assistance. There are real problems to be overcome in the matter of jurisdiction when we discuss any scheme of scholarships or bursaries for students at the university level. I accept all these considerations but I still feel there is an urgent need from the point of view of the students of future years.

It seems to me that we must have a national system of scholarships similar to that blueprinted or outlined in the recommendations of the Massey royal commission on the arts, letters and sciences submitted in 1951. In that report the recommendation was made that federal aid to education, particularly to students who desire to pursue a university career, would be advantageous to the country.

There exists at the present time a longterm shortage of professionally trained personnel. I realize also, as has been mentioned by previous speakers, that all Canadians cannot attend university. Some by reason of inclination and others by reason of natural aptitude are not suited to attend university, but for those who have the desire, for those who have the mental and natural aptitude, every opportunity should be given to pursue a career for which they have been professionally trained.

I am informed by many businessmen that such people are needed in their businesses and that the availability of such personnel is inadequate to meet present day needs. One firm in five anticipated a serious shortage of trained personnel in the years 1954 to 1956. One in four business firms have said that they are short of personnel at the present time. In addition to business administration courses that are required by many

young Canadians, mechanical and electrical engineers are in the shortest supply. A survey conducted about two years ago indicated that 39 per cent of electrical appliance manufacturing firms in Canada and 31 per cent of the chemical, oil and petroleum firms felt that their needs could not be satisfied by reason of lack of graduates or inadequately trained graduates for the particular purpose for which they were required.

The steel and iron industries throughout this country which require skilled employees of a particular type have felt the pinch. They are hard pressed for trained engineers. In recent years we in Canada have been in the forefront in the development of atomic energy. Scientists, technicians, research employees, are required to continue the work that has already been set up. I am informed that skilled personnel have had to be brought in from our neighbours to the south in order to provide some of the skill, knowledge and expert opinion that is required in connection with this branch of work. I feel that our universities should be in a position adequately to supply the needs of our atomic energy development by providing qualified personnel to fill the need. Canadian industry is suffering from its inability to find trained people to do the jobs that need to be done.

Then, as has been so well said during the afternoon by the member for Humber-St. George's, one of the important phases of university training is that of providing qualified teachers. There is a greater shortage of qualified teachers in Canada today. My view is that the fundamental necessity in all teaching is that our young people should be provided with adequate teachers. In order to provide adequate teachers we must provide adequate salaries for those persons who are trained in that vocation. The teacher shortage will perpetuate the shortage of trained technicians. I think this is so particularly in the sciences. If we have not adequate well-trained teachers we cannot hope to produce the type of skilled research scientist that is required in this country.

I come to the question of the cost of education which was mentioned earlier today. In recent years education has become more costly than it was 25 years ago, largely because of the necessity for increasing the salaries of professors and the increased costs of upkeep in carrying on the universities of the country. In some of the professional courses we find that the cost of instruments alone in one year runs as high as $350. The cost of textbooks and tuition in the university ranges from $350 to $450 or $500 a year. The average student attending university must be reasonably well clothed. I suggest that decent

clothing is not available for much less than $150 a year. Those students who are not able to reside in the particular university centre that they might desire to attend have living expenses for a school term of eight months. I suggest that under present circumstances these will not amount to less than $500. The average requirement for educational costs would therefore be from $1,500 to $1,800 per student per annum. The student also has difficulty in providing for himself part of the cost of this training.

A survey made at the University of Alberta about five years ago indicated that the average male university student earns about 51 per cent of the cost of his yearly course or in the neighbourhood of $800 out of the required $1,500. The female students are able to earn much less than are the male students. In the survey it has been estimated that the female student is in a position to earn about 40 per cent of the cost of her university training or in the neighbourhood of $600 per year. It will thus be seen that the student is short approximately $600 to $800 per annum.
While I said that it was right and proper that students should work-and work hard

in summer vacations and during Christmas holidays, I think that part-time work during the student's school term seriously interferes with studies in any course. To that consideration I add the worry and financial anxiety which accompanies any shortage in funds and which does not assist the student in any way. Rather, I suggest that it detracts a great deal from the attention which the student might give to his work. When interviewed on this subject Dr. Sidney Smith, president of the University of Toronto, stated that he thought there was a greater financial drain on those students who came from other than university centres than upon those whose homes were in the university centres which they desired to attend. Dr. Smith had this to say:

It will be increasingly difficult for the boy in Swastika and Sioux Lookout to enrol ... It will be a tragedy if universities become places where only the students who live near them are able to attend.
I suggest that is not the sort of thing that we desire in Canada.

It may be said that already a considerable amount of money is available for scholarships and bursaries throughout this country. I should like to compliment those foundations, clubs and organizations which desire to assist worthy students in furthering their university courses. The Edward Blake Memorial scholarships, the I.O.D.E. scholarships, the university women's clubs, the Massey foundation and the Leonard foundation are only a few of 82715-40i

the bursaries which have assisted many worthy students in their scholastic pursuits. But unfortunately these scholarships or bursaries do not go far enough. The average sum which is available is comparatively small. It is an insufficient portion of the student's requirements or total expenses. This situation is likely to have a tantalizing effect upon the student who, having a smaller amount available to him, will feel that he is unable to pursue further the course of his choice.

Then there is the need to assist not only the brilliant student but the very good student. There are some students who would take first place and therefore would be awarded a scholarship. But there are still those very good students who might come second or third and who would not be able to avail themselves of the opportunity to accept the present scholarships.

It is my submission that scholarships, to be worth while, must be paid in the average of $500 to $600 per annum. I take this opportunity of complimenting the government upon the introduction of legislation a few days ago to set up the Canada Council. I feel that is the vehicle which can provide scholarships of this kind in order that needy students, worthy students, may have an opportunity to pursue their courses.

I should like to bring to the attention of this house another point which occurred to me and which I think is a very serious problem to be confronted, that is the psychological barrier which is placed across the minds of needy students, those who might feel that they have no right to aspire to higher education because of the fact that they come from ordinary homes. Students of any station should aspire to the highest standard of education, if they have the ability and the desire to do so. I have read the manuscript which the students federation prepared for submission to the national scholarship committee. In reading that brief I noted that on one instance certain students of high standing who might have qualified for scholarships had not applied to avail themselves of the scholarships that were offered for competition. They were not aware of the fact that they had the right to apply for these scholarships. They were not aware of the proper method of application. I feel we must overcome the inferiority complex of some students who might feel that they should not aspire to a higher education.

I am not aware of the proportion of Canadian university students receiving aid in comparison with those receiving aid in other countries. However, I have had the opportunity of reading the brief submitted by
the national federation of Canadian university students. In their brief they had this to say, and I quote:

The proportion of all Canadian university students who receive assistance in some form or another is only about 15 per cent. In Great Britain, on the other hand, the corresponding figure is almost 75 per cent. Moreover in 1938, 14 per cent of Canadian university students received scholarships; thus we have made little progress in this respect in the last 17 years. In Britain at the present time a worthy student can obtain grants to cover the cost of both tuition and maintenance if the income of his parents is below a certain figure. In France education is virtually a state responsibility throughout. In the United States both Wisconsin and California make higher education of the best quality freely available to their residents.

I feel that in other countries, some older and some wealthier countries than our own, students are receiving aid. If we are to develop the young people of this country, and in so doing develop the national fibre of our own country, if we are to make this country a better place in which to live, then it is desirable that we should provide our students with adequate and sufficient scholarships and bursaries in order that they might assist themselves to make better citizens of themselves.

,Liberal,,Harry Peter Cavers,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d54e6b1c-79fc-4127-b9da-c703dd15e814&Language=E&Section=ALL
1881393,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.5.1.29,1957-01-24,043d4584-7dd8-4eff-b97a-e5b8349d44d6,ca.m.6101,Mr. A. M. Nicholson (Mackenzie):,,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,I should like to join hon. members in all parties, Mr. Speaker, in paying tribute to my colleague, the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) who I feel is rightly regarded as the dean of education in this chamber. Being generous he welcomes this resolution being introduced again this year by the youthful member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth). While there are not any members in the house apparently who are speaking against this resolution, it does give individual members an opportunity to speak about this very important question. I must say I cannot generate very much enthusiasm for it myself. I think it is unfortunate that the means test is suggested now in Canada for assistance on the university level. A long time ago I thought we had accepted the principle that education should be provided free to all who were capable of acquiring an education.

I think that, just as elementary education was necessary at the time of confederation, so university education is necessary now. It should be provided for those who are competent to take it. There is another weakness that is rather important. I think the suggestion that we crowd a great many more students into our universities, without first making some adequate provision for university facilities and adequate compensation for those who are teaching, is putting the cart before the horse. Nevertheless, I do
want to thank the hon. member for giving us an additional opportunity to discuss this important question.

The policies of the government nowadays point up the need for education. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) recruits high school graduates for air force personnel. He is quite prepared to spend $60,000 on training a young chap who has finished high school to fly a jet plane. I am not complaining about the expenditure of $60,000. But I think it is unfair to ask my friends down in Newfoundland to stand the cost of elementary and high school training up to the point where the youth leaves high school, and then for the federal government to come along and spend $60,000 so quickly.

The Minister of National Defence told us last June that he had spent $24 million on the ""velvet glove"". He pointed out there had been 400 scientists and specialists from industry and the forces who had acquired a good deal of practical experience in the field of air to air guided missiles. Since that time I have read that we have written off our investment in this particular field. Apparently there is no one who becomes excited about the expenditure of $24 million on a project of this sort which is then designated as an unpractical project.

Some time ago the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe) told us we will have spent $120 million on the CF-105 before it is off the assembly line. But if these machines are to be used we have to have young Canadians who have been able to go to public school and high school as well as university. Last year my colleague the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) asked the Minister of National Defence how much we were spending on the training of cadets to qualify for officers in the army, air force and navy. The reply was $3 million to $4 million for 1954; over $4 million in 1955; and $4.5 million in 1956. My colleague said that appeared to be about $30,000 per cadet. The minister replied, ""Yes, that is about correct"". He explained that costs have gone up. I submit that if the taxpayers of Canada are able to spend $30,000 to train cadets, somehow or other we have to share with the provinces and the municipalities the essential expenditures which have to be incurred before we are able to make use of our personnel in this sort of category.

Apparently, we are not short of funds in Canada, judging by some of the figures I have mentioned. Last year I received an answer to a question regarding our expenditures in Canada for tobacco, liquor and education. In 1954 we spent $475 million

on tobacco, $865 million on liquor, but only $581 million on education. It is a matter for pretty serious reflection when our per capita expenditures are $31.26 on tobacco, $56.92 on liquor and $40.26 on education.

The other day when discussing the Canada Council resolution I mentioned the percentage of the tax dollar which the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipalities spent. Members are always flattered when colleagues, particularly colleagues of other parties, ask them a few days later about their material and their sources, and I must thank the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Holowach) for paying close enough attention to my remarks to ask the question. I now wish to inform him that the Bank of Commerce commercial letter of March 1953 is my source. It gives a table showing the total Canadian tax revenue of the federal, provincial and municipal authorities. I have added these up and I find that the federal government gets 74 cents out of the dollar, the provincial governments get 15 cents and the municipal authorities, 11 cents. I was quoting from memory the other day. There has been a slight variation from year to year. I have not given the exact fractions. These are for the year 1951. I might mention that if you go back to 1939 you will find a fifty-fifty split. At that time we just gave the federal government about 50 cents out of every dollar. The municipalities fared a little better then. They had about 30 cents and the provinces about 20 cents of each tax dollar.

I have confirmed these figures by reference to the Bank of Canada statistical summary financial supplement for 1955. The 1954 figures naturally show much larger amounts collected by the federal government, the provincial governments and the munic-ipalites. They also show a distribution that makes it very difficult for the municipalities and the provinces. On the 1954 figures the federal government-I am making my calculations from the Bank of Canada figures- received about 70 cents out of each tax dollar, the provinces 16 cents and the municipalities 14 cents. You still have only 30 cents to be divided between the municipalities and the provinces. The government at Ottawa gets 70 cents. I submit that it is physically impossible for our municipal and provincial authorities to get the wherewithal to meet the crisis in the field of education.

I am indebted to a number of sources for a good deal of help. Like other hon. members, I want to refer to the very interesting conference which was held in Ottawa in November when the Canadian universities

met to discuss Canada's crisis in higher education. It is significant that the Prime Minister rated this meeting high enough to take time off to speak and to intimate that his government was prepared to take action. While action has been taken, it is much too little and, of course, it is much too late but it is better than nothing at all. It does recognize that there is a problem. I was particularly interested in some of the papers. I hold in my hand one from the director of extension of the Unversity of Montreal, one by the president of St. Francis Xavier and another one by Dr. Burchard of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the alma mater of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and one on the problems of securing staff. All these papers deserve the most careful consideration by hon. members and by all who are interested in the question of education.

I would like to make a few references to the paper by President Norman MacKenzie of the University of British Columbia. Dr. MacKenzie is a product of Dalhousie. He was President of the University of New Brunswick before the Minister of Labour, and now is president of the University of British Columbia. He presented some figures in connection with the percentage of the Canadian students who go on to take higher university work. He mentions that it would appear that between 25 per cent and 33 per cent of the population have the capacity for higher education, and goes on to say:
At the present time 7.2 per cent of the appropriate age group, 18 to 21 inclusive, are in our Canadian universities.

Is that not something to think about? Although between 25 and 33 per cent of the population have the capacity, we permit only 7.2 to proceed to university. I think I should say that although I have been to university myself, all who have been there readily recognize that you can get a university degree and still be very ignorant about a great many things. A great many who never get to university make an outstanding contribution to society also, but anyone who has been to university would consider that he had missed something if that right had been denied him. When only 7.2 of the appropriate age group in Canada are permitted to go to university it is a pretty serious situation. According to Dr. MacKenzie the figures for Russia are 19.6 per thousand of the population. For the United States the figure is 15 per thousand and for Canada it is 4.9 per thousand. The 7.2 figure would be of the appropriate age group. Dr. MacKenzie points out that if we are really to face this problem, instead of having 80,000 enrolled in universities, as we have today,

we should have between 240,000 and 315,000. By 1980, it our population goes up we should have between 375,000 and 490,000. If the provinces and the municipalities are not able to find the wherewithal now to maintain adequately the establishments that are supposed to house 80,000 and pay the salaries, how are we going to find facilities and perj sonnel to teach 240,000? Dr. MacKenzie points out:

I realize that statistics are among the most misleading materials with which human beings can work but while I do not propose to comment upon these figures, I suggest that there is plenty of food for thought in them.
The other day I had the Financial Post for November 17, 1956, and I made reference to an article on Russia by Ronald McEachern, the editor of the paper. Dr. McEachern mentioned that:

Soviet universities are hard to get into. A few prize-winners in the secondary schools go direct into university without examination. Of the remainder, around 60 per cent are flunked in their university entrance exams.
The graduate of a soviet university has about 50 per cent more formal hours of instruction behind him than the Canadian graduate.

He mentions that of all the Canadians who enter university here a little over 20 per cent survive through graduation. In Russia about 14 per cent survive and in the United States about 13 per cent. He mentions that in 1955 the Russian universities graduated about 120,000 scientists and engineers compared to about 70,000 in the United States universities. Mr. McEachern points out that there are two angles which must be associated with this fact. First, the magnitude of the Soviet economy is about one-third that of the United States so relatively the Soviet production of scientists and engineers is about five times that of the United States.

Mr. McEachern includes an interesting paragraph about a young chap who was studying at the University of Leningrad. This young man was 27 years of age and not only did he speak English very well but when he was speaking to someone from the United States he spoke as an American would and when he spoke to someone from Great Britain he spoke as people in that country do. Apparently he was somewhat puzzled by the Canadian accent. He said, ""You speak just like the Americans but you are all Canadians.""

Her Majesty whom he had met previously used the Oxford expression of the English language. Here is a chap who not only spoke his own language but had been encouraged to speak English as it is used in both Great Britain and the United States, and in addition he had been trained to

speak Italian, Spanish, French, German and some other languages. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if it is possible in a country like the Soviet union to recruit such a large percentage of young people and send them to university and train them in various fields there is no good reason for a rich country like Canada failing to grapple with the problem and leaving it to be dealt with by the municipalities and the provinces.

I am also indebted to the Canadian school trustees' association for the research work they have done under the direction of Dr. M. E. LaZerte. In the study entitled ""School Finance in Canada-1955"" Dr. LaZerte points out that education is a very different matter from what it was not so long ago when log schools were erected at a very low cost. Even in the last 25 years in the province of Saskatchewan log school houses were built with grants of $100 or $200 from the provincial government. The settlers cut their lumber out of the logs with whip saws and made desks. That sort of school accommodation is not good enough in this day and age. Dr. LaZerte also points out that school children are no longer being educated to live for the rest of their lives in one small community. They are being educated as citizens not only of their own province but of the country and the world.

I heard the speech made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) at the Canadian Club luncheon today and I was greatly interested in the fact that the minister has been able to travel over 40,000 miles since we saw him here last year. The fact that he has been able to travel to so many countries makes it important that people such as those who provided his education should not be handicapped in educating children who live in the depressed areas of Canada and are not able to attend university if the price received for the produce of the farm is not adequate. I think we have to recognize the fact that the citizen of today is a citizen of the world and he must not be handicapped because he lives in a depressed area.

In this study there is a table that gives information regarding the cost per pupil of education in the various provinces of Canada. It is surprising to find a variation from a low of $8'6.11 in Newfoundland to a high of $292.58 in British Columbia. The per capita cost again shows a wide variation. The high is British Columbia, Saskatchewan is second, Alberta is third, Ontario is fourth, New Brunswick is fifth, Manitoba is sixth, Nova Scotia is seventh, Quebec is eighth, Newfoundland is ninth and Prince Edward Island is tenth. Again we have a variation from

$45.34 per person in British Columbia to a low of $16.84 in Prince Edward Island. There is also a table giving some information regarding the relative prosperity in different parts of Canada. Questions such as the following ones were asked: Do you have a telephone? Have you an automobile? Did you have a radio in 1952 when you had to buy a radio licence? Questions such as these indicated whether or not people were too poor to afford a radio.

Another table shows the personal income by provinces, indicating the ratio. In Ontario we have a rather high average. Ontario had an average of 123 per cent. British Columbia had 120 per cent, Alberta 93 per cent, Saskatchewan 78 per cent and we come down to 53 per cent in Newfoundland and 54 per cent in Prince Edward Island.

There is also some information concerning the salaries paid to teachers which points up an impossible situation confronting the authorities in many of the provinces. For example, in Newfoundland the average teacher's salary was $1,065. The average salary is given for some of the states immediately south. The average salary for teachers in Maine was $2,115; Prince Edward Island, $1,152; New Hampshire, $2,712; Nova Scotia, $1,587; Vermont, $2,348. Going down the list we find a high average in British Columbia of $2,590 but in the state of Illinois to the south the average salary was $3,458. Again there is a wide spread between salaries paid to teachers in Canada and the United States.

My colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight) had a sessional paper back in 1952 listing the present federal expenditures on education. You find an approximate total for the year of about $20 million including the amount for the Department of Labour for apprentice training, youth training and vocational grants, the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the national research council, the Department of National Health and Welfare for professional education and post graduate training, the Department of Veterans Affairs for grants to universities and the Department of Finance for grants to universities. The total was $20,936,000. The small sum of just over $20 million was spent for the educational facilities I have mentioned, and last year $24 million was spent for the Velvet Glove, which was later discarded as useless.

I am also indebted to the Canadian teachers federation for their excellent research. They have made a study concerning the position of civil servants to point up the problem confronting those who are in the teaching profession. I have never been guilty of complaining about the salaries being paid

to civil servants. As a matter of fact, I know a great many who are staying with the public service at salaries which are a great deal less than they would command in the commercial field. But we are robbing our schools of a great many teachers and I think that this report made by the federation deserves some consideration. They say:

Of six arts graduates hired as junior administrative officers in 1946 at approximately $2,000, three of the six are now earning between $7,000 and $9,000. Of eighteen hired in 1950 at approximately $2,400, most are earning between $5,000 and $6,000; five of the eighteen are earning $6,000 to $7,000 and one is earning between $7,000 and $8,000.

They mention that those who joined external affairs and trade and commerce as foreign service officers started at $3,900 and after seven years would be receiving between $5,500 and $6,000. If those same people had gone into the teaching profession there would have been very few positions anywhere in Canada available to them at salaries at all comparable. I have here a comparison of the teacher salary schedules of some of the larger centres in Canada, and I will give the low and the high figure:

column43: are being paid when the public

column1: Ottawa offers salaries such as those I have mentioned, and when industry is offering salaries that are away out of line with those teachers are receiving.

It is particularly difficult to hold teachers in the smaller communities. A very competent science teacher up in northern Saskatchewan who had been there for seven years left last term to accept a position in Regina at a salary increase of $800 over what he had received in the small town. He was replacing a science teacher in Regina who had gone to Timmins at a salary $800 more than Regina was paying. That man in turn was replacing a teacher who had left Timmins to go to Toronto at a salary $1,000 more than was being paid in Timmins. There was a difference of $2,600 in the salary paid in a small community in northern Saskatchewan from that paid in Toronto with similar qualifications being necessary.
Mr. James Muir, president of the Royal Bank of Canada, took time in giving his
annual report to his shareholders to discuss this important question. He said:

The economic positions of all teachers has deteriorated relative to other professions of comparable training and responsibility, and relative to the working force as a whole. Thus the teacher today finds himself in the same occupational ""depressed area"" which he occupied as long ago as 1776: a member then as now of what Adam Smith called ""that unprosperous race of men commonly called men of letters"".

With the present disparity between the salaries we pay our teachers, and the salaries we pay for comparable talent elsewhere, we cannot expect to recruit or to retain enough qualified men and women to maintain our present teaching standards in our high schools and universities.

While it is all right to have a pious resolution of this sort being presented every year, a resolution which is not opposed by anyone on the government side, I submit that it is imperative that the government of Canada face up to the fact that as a result of our changing economy our municipalities and provinces have not the wherewithal to provide the facilities which will supply Canada with the educated people we must have to face the future. There is no reason why this country of 16 million people with our great natural resources, with our record of achievement in war time could not face up to the fact whatever is physically possible must be made financially possible. Something better than the plan proposed from the government side must be forthcoming if we are to meet successfully this crisis in the field of education.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Alexander Malcolm Nicholson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=043d4584-7dd8-4eff-b97a-e5b8349d44d6&Language=E&Section=ALL
1881394,ca.proc.d.1957-01-24.18.5.1.30,1957-01-24,4e3b4664-6b30-42c5-9685-4b9f9720f0f3,ca.m.7768,Mr. Guy Rouleau (Dollard):,,STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER ON ASKING OF QUESTIONS,EDUCATION,PROVISION OF NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIPS AND BURSARIES,Mr. Speaker,

at the outset of my remarks in support of the resolution put forth by the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) I should like to congratulate him heartily for having put it before the house and for having proposed it with sound argument. He has done it as a good Canadian and has dealt with the matter in a manner above party consideration and for the sole welfare of our fellow young Canadians and of Canada as a whole.

When he introduced his resolution last year the hon. member for York Centre said he was hoping for the support of all sections of the house. He got support from members of every political affiliation. I was glad, and I was also impressed at the same time by the way in which his resolution was received by the hon. members. It showed that if hon. members do not agree all the time on certain matters dealt with in the house they are all eager to promote better education and greater knowledge for the younger generation. In concluding his speech last year the hon. member for York Centre, who is known as a promoter of better understanding among the
different racial groups in Canada, made a special appeal to his colleagues of French origin, when he said, and I quote from page 571 of Hansard of January 26, 1956:
I should like to conclude my remarks in French as I am most anxious to have the support of my French-Canadian colleagues on both sides of the house.

None of the members of French origin to my left saw fit at the time to express openly in the chamber his opinion on the matter and we do not know as yet the stand of those hon. members on the matter. But on the government side of the house the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Blanchette) expressed very well I think the opinion of our French colleagues when he said in concluding his remarks on that occasion as reported on page 594 of Hansard of January 26, 1956:

The great need is for first class men to give leadership and inspiration through their own brilliant, original discoveries. The future depends not only on the continued liberality of government agencies but on the number and quality of the men induced to do research work. The greatest need is to discover and train these men, and surely the resolution of the mon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) will, if implemented, assist us to attain the aim envisaged.

Since our colleague the hon. member for York Centre, asked his French-Canadian colleagues to support him on his resolution, and since I graduated from one of our great universities not so long ago, I feel it my duty to add my voice to those who have spoken already on the matter. In doing so I feel I am doing my duty and also doing my share of what is good for my fellow citizens, my country, my province and the people I represent because they would all benefit from the implementation of such a resolution.
Mr. Speaker, the proposed resolution introduced by the hon. member for York Centre reads as follows:

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to provide national scholarships and bursaries for students at the university level who are in financial need in so far as the subject matter of this resolution is within the competence of parliament.

This proposed resolution is in complete agreement with the report of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences, as submitted to parliament in May, 1951. In this report the commissioners recommended, on page 419:
That the federal government maintain and enlarge the system of scholarships, of bursaries and of loans to undergraduates now in operation and known as the Federal-provincial Vocational Training Plan.
However, before going further into the matter and because we are dealing with

something which relates to education, may I be allowed, as a representative of a Quebec constituency, to wonder if the implementation of such legislation would interfere with provincial autonomy. In the first place, it is important to determine if this legislation is contrary to our constitution as enacted in 1867. Since we are dealing with educational matters, it is important, I think, to know if we have any right at all to discuss it and, even more to know if we may adopt legislation in aid of education.

I remember that last year, when we took up the same resolution, the Hon. George Drew, a former premier of Ontario and then leader of the federal Conservative party and of the opposition, a man who when he was a provincial premier had proclaimed himself a champion of autonomy, just like the premier of my own province, stated, as is reported on page 572 of Hansard for 1956:

The purpose of this motion, undoubtedly, is to emphasize the need for an extension, a very substantial extension, of the award of scholarships to those who seek the opportunity to take advantage of the educational facilities that our universities afford. This can be done without in any way interfering with the exclusive jurisdiction over education which rests with the provincial governments under our constitution. This can undoubtedly be worked out on a satisfactory basis of effective co-operation between the federal and provincial governments.
Now what do we find in section 93 of the British North America Act, that section which defines the powers of the provinces and confers exclusive rights in different matters? Here is what we find:
In and for each province, the legislature may exclusively make laws in relation to education, . . .

Well, Mr. Speaker, that section is clear, plain and definite about the organization of education and about the organization of our teaching institutions in the different provinces of the country, at all levels, either primary, secondary or university education. Provinces alone may enact legislation in the field of education. This was a guarantee given to them when our constitution was enacted in 1867. More particularly for the province of Quebec, it is a guarantee which was given to her perhaps primarily on account of the fact mentioned last year by the hon. member for York Centre when he said-and I quote page 598 of last year's Hansard:

I know that French Canadians are proud of their language, their customs and their traditions. They are right in feeling as they do, and I congratulate them on that score. In order to maintain this character, French Canadians mean to keep control of education in so far as it concerns them.

That is, Mr. Speaker, the main reason why French Canadians are jealous of their exclusive rights in the matter of education. They want to keep their language as well as the traditions bequeathed to them by their
ancestors, and I am convinced that the whole Canadian culture is enriched by this fact.

As I said a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, it is always a delicate matter for a federal member from the province of Quebec to deal with education. If the other provinces of confederation jealously cling to their rights in the field of education, my province, for her part, and for the reasons just mentioned, will never tolerate any encroachment on section 93 of the British North America Act which grants her exclusive rights in matters of education.

And now, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the fact that the federal government grants scholarships to our Canadian students, scholarships which are accepted by them, is an interference with the autonomy of the provinces in the field of education.

This afternoon I heard the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Girard) state that he felt the need for the establishment of this system of scholarships not only in the province of Quebec, but in the whole country. In his speech, if I am not mistaken, he said that he could not see how those scholarships could be distributed in various provinces without violating section 93 of the constitution. I respect his opinion, but I do not agree with him. As far as I am concerned, I feel that the federal government has the responsibility of helping Canadian students to pursue their courses, no matter in what province they live. We must help those students. When I was at university myself, I noticed that most of our students were from middle-class families. Many of the students of my acquaintance had to work during the summer in order to be able to pursue their studies, and several of them even had to work during hours of study. But, what about that large number of intelligent, diligent, studious, and ambitious young Canadians who cannot get higher education and who cannot go beyond college, for lack of funds. I suggest that the whole country is thus deprived of the valuable services which could be rendered by those young Canadians if they had enough funds to complete their courses.

In each of the provinces, tremendous amounts of money are spent, with reason I think, for national defence, health, research, social security and the development of our natural resources. However, Mr. Speaker, is there a greater natural resource than the intellectual potential at our disposal for making our country richer and more prosperous? We need more technicians, scientists, doctors, engineers, etc.
Mr. Speaker, we are doing a grave injustice to the nation, the Canadian family

and more particularly those born in low-income families, if we refuse to help talented students to complete their studies. I admit that the state must not substitute itself to parents, nor to the family, but it has an inescapable duty to help the family, and young Canadians. The assistance I just mentioned, which concerns us more particularly in this case, is the help to universities. That assistance could be given by various provincial governments which, on the other hand, are fairly generous in the granting of scholarships.

Moreover, in my own province, scholarships are granted annually to some students. Some foreign governments also grant university scholarships to our young men and women. There are also private concerns sufficiently conscious of their social responsibility to provide valuable scholarships annually to students from the province of Quebec or from the country as a whole. Moreover, in my own province, the St. Jean Baptiste Society, by providing honour loans renders invaluable services to young students of that province. And there are similar scholarships provided by the government of this country.

May I digress for a moment to answer the argument advanced by the hon. member for Lapointe. According to him the proposed scholarships are a threat to provincial autonomy. By the same token then we should refuse to accept scholarships provided by private enterprise, or by foreign governments. But there is no interference with provincial autonomy. These young men who receive scholarships from private enterprise or from provincial governments or from nameless associations are perfectly free to act as they wish and to benefit from the advantages provided by the scholarships in question.

Nevertheless all those scholarships which I have just mentioned are not sufficient to render justice to all our fellow citizens in every part of this country. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to see every talented, responsible, competent, studious and ambitious young Canadian provided with a higher education.

The proposed resolution introduced by the hon. member for York Centre is a long step in the right direction. That is why I am happy to support it. It does not interfere with provincial autonomy. If I were in any doubt about that, I would not support it. I am of the opinion that in certain cases the federal government may provide assistance in this field without imposing any conditions and without interfering with the
rights of the provinces in the field of education. This case which we are discussing today is such a case.

I want every young Canadian, whatever his province and racial origin, and whatever his background, to benefit equally in the field of education and every other field. This is the aim of the government in granting aid to education. It is not only in dictatorships like Russia, that certain methods are applied, not so much to help the students, but to make them the slaves of the state machine. Here, in Canada, in our democratic country, where the living is good, the sole aim of our various governments is to raise the intellectual standards of our young Canadians. As a matter of fact, their only aim is to help the nation to develop and prosper in order to exert an ever-increasing influence in the world. We want to help the less fortunate.

Some may wonder, Mr. Speaker, by what means we may determine the eligibility of students whose parents are of modest means. Well, Mr. Speaker, did we not find an adequate way of choosing those who would be eligible for the old age pension. In a field such as the one we are now considering, the government could easily find means to choose those who would be eligible for such scholarships.
At page 361 of the report which I mentioned a moment ago, one of the suggestions made by the commissioners reads as follows:

(f) That since the amendments which we are proposing in this legislation will, if they are adopted, extend the present system of scholarships to a greater number of universities and colleges, there be established an advisory council to be known as ""The University Training Advisory Council"" which will include representatives of the provincial and federal governments and of the universities.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that such a recommendation is practical and takes into account the rights of each and everyone. What we want here in Canada is to give to the greatest possible number of young Canadians an opportunity to avail themselves of our facilities for higher education so that, in the end, our whole nation may benefit by it. What we want is to give assistance to parents with large families who do not get a sufficient income but whose children have talent and wish to be educated so that they may serve the Canadian nation.

It is in that sense that I approve the resolution of the hon. member for York Centre as I am firmly convinced that the Prime Minister of Canada, who always has young Canadians in mind, will welcome this resolution. The sooner we put our education facilities within reach of a greater number of young Canadians, the better it will be for the whole country.
